SpaceX Just Got Approval to Build AI Data Centers in Space

SpaceX has received conditional approval to deploy up to one million AI computing satellites. Could solar-powered data centers in orbit help solve AI's growing energy problem? We explore how Starmind would work and the engineering challenges SpaceX still needs to overcome.

Written By
Marianne Sison
Nov 26, 2026
· 3 minute read

The next time you ask ChatGPT a question, imagine getting an answer from a computer floating hundreds of kilometers above Earth. That's essentially what SpaceX wants to make possible.

On November 25, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) gave SpaceX conditional approval to deploy up to one million satellites that would serve as data centers in space. The project, called Starmind, would use solar energy to power AI workloads in orbit.

One million satellites sounds excessive, but there's a reason SpaceX is thinking on this scale. AI needs enormous amounts of electricity, and building more data centers on Earth means finding somewhere to put them and enough power to keep them running.

SpaceX thinks part of the answer could be right above us.

How would an AI data center in space actually work?

You're probably familiar with Starlink, SpaceX's satellite internet service. Starmind would take the idea a step further by putting the computers that run AI models directly on satellites.

Advertisement

According to SpaceX's Starmind project page, its AI1 satellite is designed to support an average computing payload of 175 kilowatts and a peak capacity of 250 kilowatts. SpaceX is also working with NVIDIA to equip its satellites with Rubin GPUs and Vera CPUs.

The satellites would communicate with each other through lasers and send computing results back to Earth through the Starlink network.

As for when this might happen, the FCC has given SpaceX the following deadlines:

  • November 2033: First operational satellite.
  • November 2035: 100,000 operational satellites.
  • November 2038: 500,000 operational satellites.
  • November 2040: Full constellation.

So we have quite a few years before a million AI satellites could be circling Earth.

Why space?

Solar panels on Earth have to contend with cloudy weather and nighttime. Satellites in certain orbits can receive sunlight almost continuously, which makes space an attractive place to run computers that need a constant supply of electricity.

And AI's appetite for power isn't getting any smaller. According to the U.S. Government Accountability Office, data centers could account for up to 12% of U.S. electricity demand by 2028.

Advertisement

Moving some of that computing into orbit could ease the pressure on Earth's power grids and reduce the amount of water needed to cool data centers.

SpaceX isn't the only company exploring this idea, either.

On October 30, Google announced that a prototype satellite from its Project Suncatcher successfully ran its Gemma 4 AI model in orbit. Researchers sent the model a prompt, and it responded with a haiku about space.

Sure, writing a poem is a long way from training the next generation of AI models. But it shows that data center-class AI hardware can generate responses from orbit.

There's just one problem: space is surprisingly difficult for computers

You'd think putting a computer in the cold vacuum of space would solve its cooling problems. Turns out, it actually introduces a new one.

On Earth, computers can transfer heat to the surrounding air. In space, there's virtually no air to carry that heat away. Satellites need radiators to release excess heat, and SpaceX plans to use deployable liquid radiators for this purpose.

Then there's radiation, which can damage electronic components. And every time a satellite needs replacing, SpaceX has to manufacture another one and launch it into orbit.

Advertisement

We also have to consider what happens when Earth has another million satellites overhead. Astronomers and satellite operators have raised concerns about orbital congestion and interference with astronomical observations. The FCC has yet to approve SpaceX's proposed alternative disposal methods for certain retired satellites.

Why we're watching

SpaceX already manufactures satellites and operates its own rockets, which gives it an advantage when it comes to experimenting with orbital computing.

What we're really curious about is how much it will eventually cost to run an AI model in space compared to running the same model on Earth. If SpaceX can bring those costs down, we could have an entirely new source of computing capacity for AI.

And somewhere down the road, your AI assistant might actually be powered by a computer orbiting the planet.

items.summary: Anthropic used Claude agents to migrate its Messages API from Python to Rust. The experiment shows how AI could make software modernization more achievable and why engineers still need reliable ways to verify AI-generated code.
items.author: Marianne Sison
items.contentHtml:

Claude Helped Rebuild Its Own API, Cutting CPU Usage by 70%

Anthropic used Claude agents to migrate its Messages API from Python to Rust. The experiment shows how AI could make software modernization more achievable and why engineers still need reliable ways to verify AI-generated code.

Written By
Marianne Sison
Nov 26, 2026
· 4 minute read

What happens when an AI company asks its own AI to rebuild the software that keeps its business running?

Anthropic just gave us an answer. In a November 25 engineering report, the company revealed how it used Claude agents to rebuild its Messages API, the service that connects customers and applications like Claude Code and Cowork to its AI models.

Anthropic says the rewrite resulted in:

  • Around 70% less CPU usage per request.
  • Over 80% less memory usage per request.
  • A 20% reduction in median time to first token (how long users wait before Claude starts responding) for customer Claude Code requests.

And throughout the migration, customers could continue using Claude while Anthropic kept releasing new features.

The really interesting part? Claude took about a week to write the first version of the API's core request path. Figuring out whether it actually worked took months.

Why did Anthropic need a new API?

Advertisement

When Anthropic built its Messages API in 2023, it used Python, a programming language its researchers were already familiar with. Back then, the API had a relatively simple job: send requests to Claude and return its responses.

But as Claude gained more capabilities, the API had more work to do. It had to process increasingly complex requests, run safety checks, and handle tool calls.

Meanwhile, API traffic grew roughly 1,800 times between early 2024 and fall 2026.

Anthropic turned to Rust, a programming language known for its performance and memory efficiency. The engineering team initially tried rewriting a small portion of the API in Rust, but the performance improvements weren't enough to justify the added complexity.

As Claude got better at coding, Anthropic began to reconsider whether it could pull off a full rewrite.

Advertisement

Claude passed 98% of its tests. So what went wrong?

Here's where things get interesting. By April 2026, the new Rust API was passing around 98% of its tests. You'd probably feel pretty confident about those results, right?

Well, when Anthropic compared how the old and new APIs processed real requests before they reached Claude's models, only about a quarter of the inputs matched.

Engineers also discovered that over 100 test assertions (the conditions that determine whether a test passes) had been weakened during the migration.

The team needed to find out how the new API behaved under real-world conditions.

Anthropic used a technique called traffic shadowing, where engineers run the same requests through an existing system and its potential replacement to compare their behavior. Software engineers have used similar approaches for years to reduce the risks of changing live systems.

Since Claude can give different answers to the same question, Anthropic ran the AI model only once and shared its output between the two API implementations. The team also recorded where differences occurred rather than examining customers' conversations.

Advertisement

Whenever the system discovered a new type of bug, a coordinating Claude agent assigned another agent to investigate. The agent could recreate the problem in a separate testing environment, experiment with fixes, and send its proposed solution to an engineer for review.

Claude still needed someone to tell it when a fix was a bad idea

At one point, an agent discovered that the new API was missing the description of Claude's web search tool. Its solution? Copy the missing text into local files.

The fix passed the verification check, but an engineer rejected it. The API needed to retrieve the description from an internal service, so the proposed workaround would eventually have to be replaced.

What Anthropic did next is worth paying attention to. The team saved the engineer's feedback as an instruction for future agents. When other agents encountered variations of the same problem, they recognized it and avoided proposing another temporary fix.

Over time, engineers spent less time chasing individual bugs and more time developing the rules and automated checks that guided Claude's work.

Advertisement

Could this make expensive software rewrites more affordable?

Think about how many businesses are still running software built a decade or two ago because replacing it would cost too much or disrupt their operations.

AI coding agents could give those companies more options.

Anthropic's API migration follows other ambitious projects, including the rewrite of the Bun JavaScript runtime from Zig to Rust. Anthropic has also published guidance for running large-scale code migrations with Claude.

Of course, companies would still need engineers who understand their existing software and can establish whether its replacement behaves as expected. Anthropic spent months developing ways for Claude to check its own work before the company could trust the new API with customer traffic.

We've previously covered how Claude Code can build its own workflows around a task. Anthropic's API migration gives us a glimpse of how far companies could take this approach.

For businesses that have spent years putting off expensive software upgrades, the prospect of handing much of the coding work to AI agents could finally put those projects back on the table.

items.title: Everything That Happened in AI Today (Thursday, November 26, 2026)
items.summary: The FCC approved SpaceX's orbital AI data center constellation; OpenAI prepared shared ChatGPT usage limits; Anthropic used Claude agents to migrate its API to Rust; Amazon and Meta discussed AI shopping access; Ant released Ling-3.2-air.
items.author: Marianne Sison
items.contentHtml:
SHARE
Add The Neuron as a preferred source

Everything That Happened in AI Today (Thursday, November 26, 2026)

The FCC approved SpaceX's orbital AI data center constellation; OpenAI prepared shared ChatGPT usage limits; Anthropic used Claude agents to migrate its API to Rust; Amazon and Meta discussed AI shopping access; Ant released Ling-3.2-air.

Written By
Marianne Sison
Nov 26, 2026
· 5 minute read

SpaceX has permission to put up to one million computing satellites in orbit, and the idea of an AI data center might soon require looking up at the sky.

Welcome, humans!

AI infrastructure has officially entered the space race. The FCC has cleared a proposed network of orbital data centers, although SpaceX still has to demonstrate that computing at this scale can work beyond Earth.

Meanwhile, Anthropic published an account of how Claude helped rebuild the software that connects customers to Claude itself. OpenAI is testing a more private way to run AI for businesses, while two new assistants promise to handle work even when you're away from your desk. Apparently, the AI agents are getting comfortable working the night shift.

Let's get into it.

🆕 NEW From The Neuron

  • A 200-year-old mystery took GPT-6.2 Astra 22 minutes to investigate, according to a historian who found a reference that led to a 162-page journal.
  • Magnitude uses your SSD to run models larger than your graphics card's memory, with the company reporting 41 tokens per second on a 24 GB RTX 3090 using a 66 GB model.
  • Epochal's Time Portal lets AI agents explore archived versions of the web and make predictions before the historical answers become available.
Advertisement

Around the Horn: Thursday, November 26, 2026

SpaceX gets approval for up to one million AI satellites.

The FCC authorized SpaceX to deploy up to one million satellites for Starmind, a proposed network of computing stations in low Earth orbit. SpaceX wants satellites to process AI workloads using solar energy and transmit the results back to Earth. The authorization covers a potential network; the satellites have yet to be deployed at that scale.

The appeal is access to solar power in space, where the network could reduce its dependence on terrestrial electricity supplies. But scientists have questioned the economics and engineering, particularly how satellites would shed the heat generated by computer chips. Space debris and interference with astronomical observations are also concerns.

A million computers in space will need an extraordinary cooling system. The next milestone is a working orbital data center that can demonstrate its costs and performance against Earth-based alternatives.

Advertisement

🏆 TOP 5 NEWS (Around the Horn)

  • OpenAI will combine usage limits for ChatGPT's Chat and Work experiences. Frequent users of both may exhaust their shared allowance sooner. Instant remains available after the allowance runs out, and a wider rollout is planned for December.
  • Anthropic used Claude agents to migrate its Messages API (the interface through which applications access Claude) from Python to Rust. Agents compared the two implementations against live requests and fixed discrepancies under human review. Anthropic reports roughly 70% lower processor usage per request and a 20% shorter median wait for the first response token.
  • Amazon and Meta discussed lifting Amazon's September block on Meta's shopping agent Muse. Advertising revenue and control over search results remain under negotiation. The Decoder cites Amazon's $68.6 billion annual advertising business and reports that Muse accounts for 51% of AI-agent shopping orders. The companies have yet to announce a deal.
  • New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed a law that bans the manufacture and sale of toys powered by AI chatbots for five years.
  • Anthropic expanded in Zurich with plans for a larger office to recruit local AI researchers and establish a presence near some of the world's largest healthcare companies.
Advertisement

Honorable Mentions

  • Dario Amodei rejected accusations that he favors handing human decision-making over to AI. The Anthropic CEO also challenged Axios's reporting and criticized rival executives' positions as driven by impressions rather than substance, amid increasing automation of AI research.
  • New U.S. export rules threatened Asian AI infrastructure projects after lenders reportedly paused billions of dollars in financing associated with major Chinese cloud providers.

🍪 TOP TREATS TO TRY

  • OpenAI Private Inference: Sam Altman announced a limited customer pilot for a new offering under OpenAI Private Intelligence, intended to give businesses greater privacy when they run AI on sensitive work.
  • Ant Group's Ling-3.2-air: A multimodal AI model that processes text, images, and video and targets professional tasks through software tools. Developers can download and commercially adapt its weights under the MIT license. Ant reported a task completion rate of 61%, up from 15.7% for Ling-3.0-flash-VL on its own office-work automation test.
  • MyClaw 3.0: Build a team of always-on AI agents with separate roles and shared memory. The platform supports OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex, Hermes Agent, and Pi, plus more than 50 model options. Agents run on hosted computers and accept recurring tasks through the web or messaging apps such as Slack, Telegram, and WhatsApp.
  • Airbot: An AI chief of staff that proactively texts you about priorities across your business apps, from email and Slack to calendars and customer records. It prepares replies, meeting briefs, bookings, or CRM updates for approval through WhatsApp or iMessage.
Advertisement

🔬 AI Research & Models

  • Google DeepMind's AlphaProof Code resurfaced in coverage of how human-guided AI agents mathematically verified key security properties of the code behind Signal's encryption protocol. DeepMind originally announced the research on November 10. The technique uses mechanically checked proofs to establish specified properties of software, rather than relying solely on test cases. It does not establish the security of every component of the Signal app.

🏢 Big Tech & Major Companies

  • Google's personalized video patent drew further scrutiny over the possibility of individually generated entertainment feeds. The Verge examined the implications of endless AI-made videos tailored to viewers, although Google has yet to announce a product based on the patent.
Advertisement

🏛️ AI Policy, Governance & Safety

  • Surrey County Council adopted its first formal AI policy, which establishes rules and safeguards for the council's use of AI tools.
  • Stephen Miller's AI role remained under discussion as his involvement in the White House AI task force took shape. Former chief of staff Susie Wiles had previously played an active role in AI policy.

💡 Industry Commentary & Analysis

  • Africa's cashless payment expansion faces a new fraud challenge: AI helps criminals impersonate trusted parties and persuade people to authorize payments themselves.
  • A Cornwall Christmas market canceled all bookings after visitors and stallholders complained that the event fell short of expectations set by AI-generated promotional images.
Advertisement

Previous Around the Horn Digests

Catch up on everything you missed:

  • Wednesday, November 25, 2026: GPT-6 tackled protein design, Astra helped identify possible exoplanets, and Midjourney released Niji V8.
  • Tuesday, November 24, 2026: Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia, DeepMind improved quantum algorithms, and the NHS launched an AI cancer-screening trial.
  • Monday, November 23, 2026: AI agents reportedly designed a CPU architecture and Claude helped produce a mathematical proof.
  • Friday, November 20, 2026: Anthropic made its market debut and Gemini gained computer-use capabilities on Mac.
  • Thursday, November 19, 2026: Anthropic priced its IPO and Google unveiled Gemini 4 Neon.
  • Wednesday, November 18, 2026: OpenAI introduced GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, while Google revised Gemini privacy controls.
  • Tuesday, November 17, 2026: OpenAI invited independent safety evaluators into its labs and Apple tested Siri AI usage limits.
Advertisement

That's a Wrap

That's 18 stories in today's roundup. If you made it to the bottom, you've officially logged more AI news than a satellite that's still waiting for launch day.

For the daily five-minute version, subscribe to The Neuron. We read the AI news so you don't have to.

See you tomorrow.

P.S. Know someone who'd enjoy this roundup? Forward it to them and tell them to subscribe here.

items.contentHtml:
Henry Shukman (@henryshukman) is an authorized Zen master in the Sanbo Zen lineage, one of only a few dozen in the world, and spiritual director emeritus of Mountain Cloud Zen Center in Santa Fe, New Mexico. He is the co-founder and lead teacher of The Way, a meditation app that takes you down a single guided path, step by step, instead of handing you a thousand choices. You can try it free for 30 days (no credit card required) at TheWayApp.com/Tim.

Before teaching, Henry was an award-winning poet and novelist. He is the author of the Zen memoir One Blade of Grass and of Original Love: The Four Inns on the Path of Awakening. He holds degrees from Cambridge and St Andrews. You can find him at henryshukman.com.

😸 3 Microsoft execs explain their AI plan

Written By
Ron Reinfeld
Co-Authors
Ron Reinfeld

Sergey Novikov

Mario Vuksan

Welcome, humans.

I went to Microsoft Ignite with a question: When Microsoft says it’s building AI into everything, how do the people making the stuff decide what belongs where? I sat down with three of them for this week’s episode. Somewhere between GitHub and Azure, we got into how I cook chicken. I promise that part makes sense.

GitHub’s Kyle Daigle walked me through a decision your laptop can make for you. Copilot’s Sergey Fayfer and I found a decision I’d like to keep for myself. And Azure’s Arun Ulag told me what happens when you give Satya Nadella access to a new tool on Friday afternoon. You hear from him on Saturday.

My favorite moments:

  • (1:25:50) The Saturday email from Satya. He wanted to compare returns on invested capital across seven tech companies. By the time he emailed Arun, he had a working dashboard. Listen for what Copilot had to do with ten years of PDFs to get there.

  • (39:00) My personal AI knows how I cook chicken. My work AI knows my calendar. Sergey and I talk through what I’d actually want to carry between the two. My cooking preferences are easy. My employer’s data makes the reverse trip a much trickier question.

  • (11:40) Your laptop gets the next turn. Kyle explains how GitHub Copilot Fusion can hand a piece of work to a local model when the machine and the task are a good fit. If you always pick the biggest model and leave it there, this one’s for you.

Why watch? The next time an AI tool asks for access to your files, you’ll have three better questions to ask: Where will the work run? What does it need to know? And when does it need my OK?

Watch or listen: YouTube | | Apple Podcasts

P.S. At 27:30, Kyle gets into a real software project for making ketchup packets at home. I did not have condiment manufacturing on my Ignite bingo card.

Keep scrolling for a closer look at Satya’s dashboard, Pika’s AI actors taking direction, and Monday’s live discussion about Jensen Huang’s return.

Additional Resources: How do you get from a stack of PDFs to a dashboard?

Arun’s story has a detail I love: Satya asked a finance question. He didn’t specify a database, a chart type, or a place to put the files. Here’s what Arun says happened behind the scenes.

First, Copilot gathered the financial filings and put them in OneLake, which Arun describes as OneDrive for your data. Next, Fabric ran jobs to pull the numbers out of the PDFs. Then it built a semantic model, the layer that tells software what a business measure means, and an app to display the results.

About 30 to 35 minutes later, Satya got a link. The part Arun cared about was where that link led: the dashboard ran inside Microsoft’s own Fabric environment, where it could draw on internal figures alongside the public filings.

Explore Microsoft’s Azure announcements from Ignite →

Four recent interviews and episodes we think you’ll love.

2. How much AI history have you already forgotten?

CEO John Acunto explains the move from music to visual AI agents for businesses. If you’re considering a customer-facing agent, listen for who gets to keep what it learns from the conversation.

Watch / Listen: YouTube | | Apple Podcasts

4. For anyone who’s had to teach a robot a new job

Standard Bots CEO Evan Beard explains what a factory robot can learn by watching a person do the work. The interesting part comes when the next object lands a little differently. That’s where a good demo meets a real production line.

Watch / Listen: YouTube | | Apple Podcasts

Jensen Huang’s return and the claims about an AI-assisted Riemann proof gave us plenty to talk about. Catch the replay here.

items.title: Magnitude Uses Your SSD to Run AI Models Bigger Than Your Memory
items.summary: Magnitude says a 24 GB RTX 3090 generated 41 tokens per second with a 66 GB Qwen model. The open-source engine keeps frequently used weights in memory and streams the rest from an SSD. How soon you see the first word is a separate question.
items.author: Corey Noles
items.contentHtml:
SHARE
Add The Neuron as a preferred source

Magnitude Uses Your SSD to Run AI Models Bigger Than Your Memory

Magnitude says a 24 GB RTX 3090 generated 41 tokens per second with a 66 GB Qwen model. The open-source engine keeps frequently used weights in memory and streams the rest from an SSD. How soon you see the first word is a separate question.

Written By
Corey Noles
Nov 25, 2026
· 3 minute read

A 66 GB AI model has no business fitting on a graphics card with 24 GB of memory. And yet Magnitude says it got that model, a 2-bit version of Qwen 3.8 Flash Next, generating at 41 tokens per second on an RTX 3090 with 64 GB of system RAM and a PCIe 4.0 SSD. The GPU only had to hold the parts it was most likely to use. Magnitude’s benchmarks

That’s the idea behind Magnitude, the open-source inference engine Tom Greenwald introduced for Macs and PCs. It treats the GPU, system RAM, and SSD as three places to store model weights, then moves pieces between them as the model runs. Your SSD is still the slowest of the three. The trick is giving the GPU as few reasons to wait for it as possible. Greenwald’s launch post · Magnitude’s open-source repo

How a 66 GB model runs on a 12 GB card

Qwen 3.8 Flash Next is a mixture-of-experts model. Part of it is divided into blocks called experts, and the model routes each token through a small selection of them. For Qwen, that’s 10 out of 512 routed experts per token. A different token can call for a different set, so the engine still needs access to all of them. Qwen’s benchmark configuration

Advertisement

Magnitude keeps the shared layers and most-used experts in GPU memory. It caches the next tier in system RAM and fetches the rest from an NVMe SSD, trying to bring experts into memory before the GPU asks for them. When an expert arrives in time, the GPU can keep working. When the GPU has to wait for a disk read, generation can slow down. How often that happens depends on what fits in memory and which experts the workload needs. Magnitude’s explanation of expert streaming

The RTX 3060 result makes the case for this approach. Magnitude reports 17 tokens per second with the same 66 GB Qwen build on a 12 GB card, 32 GB of RAM, and a PCIe 3.0 SSD. The model file is larger than the machine’s GPU memory and system RAM put together. At the other end, Magnitude reports 17 tokens per second with a 249 GB DeepSeek V4.1 Flash build on a 32 GB RTX 5090 with 128 GB of RAM and a PCIe 4.0 SSD. Magnitude’s hardware results

The number I’d want before running an agent

Those are Magnitude’s own decode figures, measured with a 64K context setting and speculative decoding enabled. They tell you how fast the engine produces tokens once generation is underway. You’ll still wait while the model processes your input, and an agent can repeat that cycle every time it reads a file or gets a tool result. A fast stream of text tells you little about how long the whole job will take. Magnitude’s benchmark methodology

Advertisement

I plan to test Magnitude myself over the next few days on my RTX 4000 Ada and on a Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra with an NVIDIA RTX Spark N1X and 128 GB of unified memory. I can’t wait to see what that laptop does. Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra specs

I’ll start with the same 2-bit Qwen build on both machines. First, I’ll ask it to summarize a paragraph. Then I’ll give it a long transcript and ask for the same length of summary. With the model already loaded and a fresh chat for each run, I’ll record time to first token and generation speed. The first number tells you how long you’re staring at a blank response. The second tells you how quickly it fills in.

For people building local agents, the practical change is a bigger menu of models on the hardware they already own. A model that used to be too large to try could be fast enough for a background job that processes sensitive files on-device. Interactive work has a different threshold. If I’m waiting on an agent to answer a question about a codebase, I care how soon it gives me something I can use. That’s the benchmark I’d like to see next. The Neuron’s look at local-first agents

Advertisement

Related reading

  • Our walkthrough uses LM Studio to show how to pick a model, load it, and read its speed metrics. Your guide to running powerful AI models on your own laptop
  • DeepSeek’s design tackles another source of memory pressure by reducing how much state the model stores as a conversation grows. How DeepSeek V4.1 Flash shrinks its persistent KV cache

Corey Noles

Corey Noles is the Host of The Neuron: AI Explained podcast and Managing Editor of AI and Experimental Content at TechnologyAdvice, where he leads the charge in testing and refining emerging content strategies across the company's portfolio.

items.title: The deep work routine that changed my life
items.summary: If you can spend 8 hours building someone else’s dream, you can spend 1 hour building your own. But how you use that 1 hour determines everything. If you were to focus on the one thing that leads to the most progress toward your ideal life, for 1 hour a day, first thing in the…
items.author: DAN KOE
items.contentHtml:
If you can spend 8 hours building someone else’s dream, you can spend 1 hour building your own.

But how you use that 1 hour determines everything.

If you were to focus on the one thing that leads to the most progress toward your ideal life, for 1 hour a day, first thing in the morning when your mind is clear and distractions are minimal, for 6-12 months, that’s 365 potential hours invested in the life you want. You can do far more than you think in that amount of time.

For most of my life, I worked 2-4 hours a day.

I feel like influencers flexing their millions put a sour taste in people’s mouth, but for the sake of results, I’ll flex a bit. Those 2-4 hours are exactly how I built an audience that’s closing in on 5 million followers across all platforms, and I’ve made just around $10m from my personal brand alone, not my other companies. That’s the time I used to put out posts, articles, newsletters, YouTube videos and podcasts. That’s also how I wrote 2 books with 2 more on the way - no AI writing involved.

And when I had a 9-5 job, I didn’t have 12 hours a day to make my side business a success. I had 1-2 hours, and a few more on the weekend.

If you want the stupid simple deep work routine, go ahead and skip to the last section of this letter.

But if you have a greater attention span than a goldfish, and understand that the “actionable advice” you crave so bad means nothing without context, I would encourage you to read every section. Bookmark this if you are short on time and set a reminder to come back to it.

You are free to skip to the later sections, but if you have a greater attention span than a goldfish, I would encourage you to read every section. Bookmark this if you are short on time and set a reminder to come back to it.

Let’s discuss why busy people end up on the bottom, why pursuing anything but your life’s work is a waste of time - especially as jobs go extinct slowly then all at once, and finally, how to structure your day not only for maximum productivity, but for maximum leverage.

Enjoy.

I – For most of human history, the busiest people were the lowest status.

Aristotle said we work so that we can have leisure, and that without it no one becomes wise.

Seneca said that the busiest people were often the least accomplished, because they spent their days on everything except their own lives.

Leisure used to be a mark of status while busyness was a mark of obligation. Busyness belonged to slaves, serfs, and laborers who worked from sunrise to sundown.

At some point in the last century, that flipped.

“I’m so busy” became a badge of honor, even when most people knew they were working on nothing meaningful, with nothing to show except time invested in someone else’s vision.

I believe that this flip will happen again.

Soon, it will be seen (more than it already is) as low status to be glued to your computer, sending messages back and forth to Claude all day. We all have big dreams and aspirations, but it requires a certain level of creativity to achieve those dreams without 12 hours of “hard work” as your main strategy.

Time for thinking, strategizing, and creativity will be the mark of high status. In many cases, it will be reserved for the rich.

Now, when I say I worked 2-4 hours a day above, that was somewhat of a lie.

As a writer, if you were to add up the time I spend walking, reading, learning, thinking, and even sleeping... I “work” 24 hours a day. Because all of those activities fuel the quality of my writing, and one hour of writing a day can reach millions of people, and if a fraction of those people purchase from me or my business, I can make millions of dollars. Some people can’t wrap their head around this, because their income is tied to their time spent doing labor. They do not earn from the creative ability of their mind, which will only become more and more of a requirement in the future.

This is mostly why we’re building Eden. It is where you grow your audience and build a digital business. It’s where you sell your products, save all your ideas and bookmarks, and turn those unique ideas into content. If that content gets traction, then you promote your work and get paid for it. There’s a ￼30 day sprint that walks you through all of this. It’s a measly $5.

II - The historical normal is to be self-employed, working a job was a temporary glitch.

Specialization is in fact only a fancy form of slavery wherein the ‘expert’ is fooled into accepting his slavery by making him feel that in return he is in a socially and culturally preferred, ergo, highly secure, lifelong position.

– Buckminster Fuller

During Industrialization, everything became a factory.

Schools included.

The sole purpose of a school system is to prepare children for the jobs of its time, and the jobs at the time were factory jobs - and I can’t help but wonder how education is going to look when the jobs of our time drastically change, or just become meaningless. I believe we are heading into a Second Renaissance, but I’ll save that for later.

Bells marked the start and end of the day. Kids are grouped by age, like batches. Subjects are split up, like an assembly line. Grades and tests were quality checks. Students were rewarded for doing what they were told, on someone else’s schedule, toward someone else’s goal.

Everyone reading this likely went through this system.

And since the mind is shaped through conditioning, and our identity latches onto that which provides us security and comfort, we are all in some way unconsciously tied to a style of work that was only an experiment.

The modern concept of a job is only 100-200 years old. Homo sapiens are 300k years old. Working 9-5, being paid a wage, and having your worth attached to your title is not normal, and it definitely isn’t beneficial to how our brains are wired. Life quickly becomes mechanical.

Work used to mean owning your work.

In 1800, most Americans were farmers, farm workers, or ran a family business. The word “job” meant one piece of work until the late 1700s. It did not mean 40+ years of your life.

The Renaissance ideal was the “universal man” who did many things well. Craftsmen worked under a guild, progressing from apprentice to journeyman to master. “Masterpiece” first meant the work you made to prove you were a master.

I believe history is repeating itself, as it always does, and we are entering the era of the craftsman. A craftsman’s worth was determined by how they used their tools. Today a laptop, the internet, and AI are cheap tools anyone can own. The craft they pursue, their vision for their work, and obsession over the details is what makes the difference. Anyone can build anything, but attention is finite, so only those who treat their work as their life’s work, pouring their heart and soul into what they do will rise above.

In The Third Wave, Alvin Toffler had a similar theory.

He called it the Electronic Cottage, which he saw as the third wave of work.

The first wave was farming, people mostly made what they used. The second wave was the factory, which split people into producers and consumers. The third wave is information and computers, where work moves back home. We once again become creators.

His argument is that a lot of work was “cottage industry,” where families spun, wove, and made goods at home. The factory pulled work out of the home and into one big building. He predicted that computers would reverse that and bring work home again (I’m sitting in my office, in my underwear, at 10:09 am, writing this, by the way).

During the First Wave most people consumed what they themselves produced. They were neither producers nor consumers in the usual sense. They were instead what might be called prosumers.

I believe that’s what a creator is. Not a content creator per se, although social media is where a creator would find their audience in today’s world, until social media is replaced with another form of media.

A friend I have online sells cotton apparel because he is against polyester clothing. I can get my apparel from him. Another online friend teaches philosophy, I can get my education from him. Another sells software. Another sells and ships baked goods. So on and so forth. I can pursue my interests and find a wedge in a digital tribe that I can contribute best to - we call this a “niche.” The creator economy has had its ups and downs, but at the end of the day, I see it as a digital society where we can learn, earn, create, and contribute to each other’s lives. That is the modern renaissance lifestyle.

Marshal McLuhan called this the global village where our specialist and fragmented civilization begins to retribalize.

If you have any desire to pursue your interests, do what you want with your life, and become adaptable enough to not have to worry about job loss:

Subscribe now

III – I’m begging you to go all in on your life’s work

There are almost 7B people on this planet. Someday, I hope, there will be almost 7B companies.

– Naval Ravikant

If you are up to date with tech and AI, you’ve probably heard something like this:

Software is dead. Info is dead. Companies are dead. Everything is dead. Everyone is just going to build their own software and get the information they need with AI.

So what do you do when it feels worthless to even start?

First, everything is not dead. Social media is great at keeping you complacent.

Jake Paul, of all people, has pivoted to the info space - look at his business YouTube channel, because frankly they are still the best way for creators to monetize, even when AI has all information (hint: if someone doesn’t know what to ask AI, and they don’t know what good advice looks like, then they won’t get the information they need - humans will be proxies for education and information for people who resonate with their point of view.)

Second, considering people don’t even cook their own food and pay far too much for Uber Eats, I highly doubt they will build their own software. Building a tool to replace a $10-20 subscription instead of focusing on one lever-moving action that makes $1000 an hour is foolish.

Plus, I would rather pay someone who’s made it their life’s work to create the best, say, content scheduling app than build one myself (although that’s what I built), there aren’t going to be 1000 content schedulers in the future. I would rather pay the craftsman who is going to obsess over the details, because obsessing over the details myself would just distract me from moving my own priorities forward.

“Anyone can build anything” is the greatest distraction of our time when we are all painfully aware that long-term focus on one meaningful goal with high potential payoff is what leads to the greatest result and most fulfillment. The future isn’t everyone building everything, but everyone building their one thing and trading with each other. A global village.

In that case, the best course of action is to discover what your life’s work is, and use the tools available to you to build it and spread it to an audience of people who resonate with your mission.

Your “life’s work” is work that allows you, specifically, to unleash the full creative ability of your mind, so that you have a vessel for your potential and contribute to humanity at your fullest.

It is difficult to label exactly what your life’s work is. It isn’t something you need to name. People get hung up on knowing exactly what they do as their life’s work. This isn’t a job. It’s not a set string of tasks. It’s a path in the unknown. It is a way of life where your learning, thinking, and acting are in harmony, and you are contributing to yourself and the world in a way only you can.

That means the work you choose must be something you have a deep interest in, and allows for near-infinite upward movement.

In other words, you’ll probably have to become an entrepreneur of some form.

Because with a “job,” as we define it today, there tends to be a low skill ceiling. You reach a point where you’ve learned enough to coast, the work becomes repetitive and mundane, and you get bored with no freedom to grow into your next shell, until even that shell becomes too constrained, so you overindulge in degenerative activities.

The question then is:

How do you find the thing that you, specifically, were meant to do?

And how do you turn that into your work so that you can comfortably survive and reap the meaning that comes from impacting others?

IV – One hour a day. One meaningful project. One vision for the future.

Code and media are permissionless leverage. They’re the leverage behind the newly rich. You can create software and media that works for you while you sleep.

– Naval Ravikant (again)

To tie this all together:

  • Non-busyness is the new mark of status, and it is required for true creative thinking

  • The pendulum is swinging back to self-employment and entrepreneurship being the norm, take advantage early

  • If you want to compete, you must pursue your life’s work - you must dedicate yourself to one thing, avoid distractions, not try to build everything, and focus on quality and craftsmanship - or else you will be bucketed in with everyone else producing slop

All of these things are arguing the importance of one thing - leverage.

Leverage is getting more of a result per hour of effort, because something other than your time keeps doing the work after you stop.

Creative thinking, entrepreneurship (freedom of work), and experience are necessary pre-requisites to leverage. It is the only way to compete in a world of ‘everyone can do anything.’ Committing to anything but your life’s work is a death sentence.

At a job, the employee mindset you adopt conditions your mind to be anti-leverage. And most people have this way of thinking deeply ingrained in them.

Most people need to be told what to do. They have difficulty accepting that anything can be figured out through the process of trial and error - that’s how the world as we know it came to be, and people did in fact do incredible things before there were instruction manuals for doing them.

Most people can’t dissociate time from money. They see a task’s worth as flat, because as long as they show up for 40 hours a week, they’ll get a paycheck. They cannot fathom that there is some way to make an entire months worth of their income in an hour, if they simply focused only on the tasks with the highest leverage.

As an example, I can publish an X article, and that article can somehow amass a freakish 260 million views, and 1% of those people visit a product page, and 1% of them purchase that product for $150, that’s $3.9 million.

But those are crazy numbers.

What if you post consistently, to the point of generating a few hundred thousand impressions a month (not that hard to do, if you learn and actually try and don’t quit after 2 weeks - it takes longer than 2 weeks to get good at something silly), and you understand that you can tweak the post, the landing page, and the offer to increase conversions to an “okay” 2.5%, then that’s more money than you’d know what to do with.

That’s leverage.

You have posts that generate traffic, and you have a product that sells while you sleep. Both are in alignment with your life’s work.

It’s like dating. If you (the product) are valuable, but you don’t put yourself in front of men/women (traffic), then you aren’t going to get a date. It’s obvious. If you (the product) aren’t valuable, and you put yourself in front of a ton of men/women (traffic) then you probably won’t get a date either, at least not one that you want.

Outside of finding what your life’s work is, those are quite literally the only things that matter. Improving what you offer - a product or service - and iterating on your posts, ads, sponsorships or whatever else you use to generate traffic. For someone who doesn’t have capital to invest or a proven offer, your best bet is organic posts on social media.

I made this Life’s Work Finder AI that interviews you to find your life’s work, then tells you what your content topics could be, and what first product you could sell, then helps you set it all up in Eden to start posting and selling.

Translating this - what do you actually do?

Block out 1 hour a day.

Work on 1 meaningful project.

Aim for 1 vision for your future.

Take it 1 day at a time, for 1 year.

1 hour of deep work is better than 0 hours, and you can drastically change your life in 365 hours.

Then, increase to 2 hours, maybe even 3. You’ll have other work to do as well, but I’m more worried about focusing on executing the highest priority, highest leverage task first thing in the morning to ensure it gets done.

Because when was the last time you asked yourself, before you started working, if I were to do one thing today, what would take me the furthest to my goal?

Probably never.

So what do you do during that one hour?

If you don’t have a product, build one during that hour.

Once you have the product, start writing content.

That’s how businesses are built right now.

Look at Jordan Peterson, Andrew Huberman, and the rest. They probably don’t register themselves as “content creators” or “personal brands.” They have a deep obsession with their interests, they share their learnings and worldview with the world in hopes of helping people.

They use content as the way to capture attention, because that’s where the attention is right now. It doesn’t matter if you don’t like social media - good luck building a business with the newspaper or radio as your distribution.

I’ll write more on this in future articles.

For now, you can find more of my writing here, use Eden to grow your audience and start an online business here, and use the Life’s Work Finder to implement everything we talked about here.

– Dan

items.title: Epochal Time Portal Tests AI Forecasting on the Past Web
items.summary: Epochal’s Time Portal sends AI agents back to an archived version of the web so they can make forecasts before the answers appear online. The bigger payoff would be an AI that spots trouble early enough for people to act.
items.author: Corey Noles
items.contentHtml:
SHARE
Add The Neuron as a preferred source

Epochal Time Portal Tests AI Forecasting on the Past Web

Epochal’s Time Portal sends AI agents back to an archived version of the web so they can make forecasts before the answers appear online. The bigger payoff would be an AI that spots trouble early enough for people to act.

Written By
Corey Noles
Nov 25, 2026
· 4 minute read

Ask an AI to call an election the day before polls close. Give it the polls, the local reporting, and the campaigns’ final pitches. Then watch it open a news article published that morning, scroll past an update added the next night, and find out who won. Congratulations, your AI is great at reading election results.

Epochal wants to build AI that can tell us what’s likely to happen before it happens. Its first product, Time Portal, tackles the problem you run into when you try to measure that skill. How do you give an AI access to the internet without giving it the answer?

Guodong Zhang, Zihang Dai, and Manuel Kroiss, all members of xAI’s July 2023 founding team, unveiled Epochal on November 24. Bloomberg reports that the three left xAI after its February merger with SpaceX and that Zhang is personally investing $100 million, according to one unnamed source. Epochal declined to comment on funding. xAI’s original launch roster · Bloomberg’s reporting

Give the AI yesterday’s internet

Advertisement

A search engine’s date filter sounds like it should solve the election problem. But an article can keep its original publication date long after an editor has added the result. In a study published at ACL, date-filtered Google searches turned up at least one page with major post-cutoff information for 71% of the forecasting questions the researchers tested. For 41%, a page gave away the answer outright. The ACL study on date-filtered search

Time Portal lets a developer pick a date and time, then gives an agent archived pages captured by that point. If the agent opens that election story, it can get the earlier version, assuming Epochal has it. Developers can also run the agent in a sandbox that sets its clock to the chosen time and routes web requests through the archive. Epochal says the archive holds more than a trillion pages across 30-plus years, with some frequently updated pages captured as often as a minute apart. What matters for any given forecast is whether the archive caught the specific sources the agent needs. The company released Python and Rust SDKs, a command-line tool, and an MCP server. Epochal’s launch post · Developer repository

There’s still one place yesterday’s answers can hide. If a model learned who won the election during training, rewinding its browser won’t make it forget. Historical replays can still help developers compare approaches quickly. FutureSearch already does this with a frozen set of pages for each question. Developers can change which sources an agent consults or how it combines forecasts, then score a new run the same day because the real outcomes are already on record. How FutureSearch runs historical tests

Advertisement

What Epochal’s first test showed

Epochal ran agents on 347 live questions from Kalshi and Polymarket, then reran those questions weeks later with Time Portal set to the original forecast times. The errors in the two runs had a correlation of 0.98. In plain English, the questions that tripped up the agents live tended to trip them up again in the replay. That number measures how closely the error patterns tracked each other. To see whether practice in Time Portal makes an agent better, you’d need to watch it make new forecasts and see how they score. Epochal’s replay experiment

What a good forecasting AI could actually do

Imagine you run a factory and a port slowdown threatens a critical shipment. An agent could follow port notices, carrier updates, and local reporting, then estimate the chance your parts arrive more than a week late. If that probability rises from 15% to 40%, you might pay to reroute one shipment while there’s still time. A city could use the same kind of system to track the odds that a transit project misses its opening date and decide when to line up extra bus service.

Advertisement

For that to work, the numbers have to mean something. Across many events the AI puts at 30%, roughly three in ten should happen. It also has to update early enough for someone to act. An alert that arrives after your last chance to reroute the shipment is just a very punctual explanation of why you’re out of parts.

That’s the next test for Epochal. Put a forecaster trained with Time Portal up against skilled humans or prediction-market odds on the same unresolved questions, at the same time. Publish the scores alongside an accounting of which sources the archive captured and where it came up short. As we’ve seen in forecasting contests, who wins can depend on which questions get asked and how the forecasts are scored. The Neuron’s look at how AI forecasting is scored

A reliable forecaster could give more teams something that usually takes a dedicated analyst to produce and keep current. A running estimate of what might go wrong, what changed the odds, and how much time they have to do something about it.

Advertisement

Related reading

  • See how Prophet Arena scores AI predictions on real events that are still unfolding. Can AI predict the future?
  • Explore a different approach to business forecasting, built around structured company data such as sales and customer records. ChatGPT can summarize data. Can it predict what happens next?

Corey Noles

items.title: The “facts” you learned at school that other countries tell differently
items.summary: “There’s an old expression that goes like this: If you ask a fish about water, the fish will say, ‘What water?’ Because it’s just around them, and a lot of our ideas and assumptions about the world are like that. We just float in them. We’ve never necessarily examined them…
items.author: Jonny Thomson
items.contentHtml:
“There’s an old expression that goes like this: If you ask a fish about water, the fish will say, ‘What water?’ Because it’s just around them, and a lot of our ideas and assumptions about the world are like that. We just float in them. We’ve never necessarily examined them because it’s sort of obvious.”

Last week, I spoke with Jimmy Wales — the man responsible for Wikipedia, the darling of students all over the world since 2001. Our conversation meandered pleasantly over philosophy, technology, cryptocurrency, politics, history, and more. (Big Think members can get first access to watch the full video at this link.)

But Wales’s fish parable hit me. What “water” do I swim in? Of course, you can take this two ways. First, the water can be seen broadly: the slightly opaque “ways of thinking” we operate under in the 21st-century post-Enlightenment West. We’ll park that discussion for another day. But we can also see this “water” more practically: What specific facts or pieces of information do I think I know, but aren’t as “obvious” as I thought?

I feel as if it’s my philosophical duty to raise doubts where no doubts existed before. And so, here are five “facts” that are actually far more disputed in life — and on Wikipedia — than you might have thought.

1. The Wright brothers invented the airplane

Of course! If you’re feeling really bookish, you could add “Kitty Hawk, December 1903.” The story of the Wright brothers is such a Hollywood-ready fact that it’s almost impossible to forget: two bicycle makers, one windy beach, and twelve seconds in the air.

Unless you went to school in Brazil. Brazilians have two objections to the Wright brothers’ claim: First, no official watched their 1903 flight. Second, the Wright Flyer needed a rail to take off. So, Brazilians give credit for the airplane’s invention to Alberto Santos-Dumont, who flew his 14-bis biplane near Paris in the autumn of 1906. He did so in public with Aéro-Club officials on hand to measure it, and he took off on his own wheels.

Wikipedia doesn’t come down on either side. It has a whole article for the rival claims, where the Wrights and Santos-Dumont have to share the page with Gustave Whitehead, Samuel Langley, and a few other men who were absolutely, definitely first.

2. Alan Turing cracked the Enigma code

In 2021, I wrote my book Mini Philosophy, and it was published with three mistakes. First, I wrongly claimed Christopher Nolan directed The Joker. (It was Todd Phillips.) Second, I attributed a quote to Aristotle that actually came from a scholar of Aristotle. But the third mistake, by far and away, was the one that caused the most uproar. I got emails, letters, and pretty intense direct messages. I had claimed the British had cracked the Enigma code. It was Alan Turing and the geniuses of Bletchley Park, surely? That’s what I’d grown up with.

But Enigma was first broken in Warsaw at the end of 1932 by a 27-year-old Polish mathematician named Marian Rejewski. That’s almost seven years before the war began. He and his colleagues, Jerzy Różycki and Henryk Zygalski, spent the 1930s reading German messages. Then, in late July 1939 — five weeks before the invasion of Poland — they invited British and French codebreakers to a forest outside Warsaw and showed them how it was done.

None of this is a secret. Rejewski’s Wikipedia page sums up what he is known for in a single line: “Solving the Enigma machine cipher.” And GCHQ’s own history is happy to say that the first British Bombe owed a great deal to Turing’s meeting with Polish codebreakers. Turing was still a genius, but he was also standing on Polish shoulders.

I mean, really, this fact isn’t so much “disputed” as just “Jonny, you were wrong.”

3. There are seven continents

I kind of knew all the other facts on this list before researching this article, but this one was a shock. Seven. There are seven continents. I admit there’s a bit of controversy around “Australia” vs. “Australasia” vs. “Oceania,” but we all agree on seven, right?

But in Greece and much of the Romance-speaking world, from Lisbon to Lima, children learn that there are six continents, because North and South America are a single continent called “America.” Russian children learn six as well, but a different six: The Americas stay apart, but Europe and Asia are merged into Eurasia. Something a lot of anthropologists and geologists do as well. And the Olympic flag has five rings for five inhabited continents — one America again, with Antarctica left off altogether until the penguins whip together a bobsled team.

The Wikipedia article doesn’t pick a winner. There are, it says, up to seven continents and as few as four. Which means that somewhere, right now, two perfectly well-educated adults are arguing in a pub about something they each learned before they could tie their shoelaces. And they’re both right.

4. The United States won the War of 1812

That depends on who you ask, and in this case, there are three people you could ask.

Ask a Canadian, and you’ll hear about a plucky Canada seeing off an American invasion. Ask an American, and it’s the “Second War of American Independence.” Ask a Brit, and you’ll mostly get a blank look because, for Britain, it was a sideshow to the real business of beating Napoleon. And we’ve loved to hate the French ever since.

In a 2009 poll, 37% of Canadians said Canada won, and only 9% gave it to the United States. Not every American would argue. “By my count,” the American historian Donald Hickey said, “we lost the War of 1812, and we lost Vietnam.”

And Wikipedia? Its editors have spent years on the question. There is a dedicated discussion page titled “Who Won?” and then there was a formal mediation case. And after all that, the article settles on calling the entire debate “inconclusive.”

5. The Second World War began in 1939

On September 1, 1939, Germany invaded Poland. “This country is at war with Germany,” the British Prime Minister, Neville Chamberlain, said at the time. And so, that’s when the Second World War started.

But in Russia, the war that matters — the “Great Patriotic War” — began on June 22, 1941, when Germany invaded the Soviet Union. In China, it starts much earlier. In 2017, the Ministry of Education announced that the war against Japan would be counted from 1931, not 1937, and an 8-year war became a 14-year war overnight.

Wikipedia keeps a whole archive of editors arguing about this, and at one point, the article itself cited 1937 as the start. My favorite contribution comes from an editor who backed 1939 on entirely practical grounds: They said that if Wikipedia said 1937, a teenager somewhere would copy it into their homework and be marked wrong.

Which is, I think, the whole point. So often, the “right” answer is simply the one your teacher is expecting. But both the teacher and the student are stuck in the same problem. As Georg Hegel, Jimmy Wales, and Pink Floyd all knew, we are all just fish swimming in a fishbowl, and no one’s commenting on the water.

This article The “facts” you learned at school that other countries tell differently is featured on Big Think.

items.title: Reflections on the Life in Perspective Book Tour
items.summary: A few days ago, I got back from my first official book tour for the launch of my new book Life in Perspective . I’ve traveled to promote my past books, but going on a proper book tour across three cities was something altogether different. In every room and conversation, I…
items.author: Tiago Forte
items.contentHtml:
A few days ago, I got back from my first official book tour for the launch of my new book Life in Perspective.

I’ve traveled to promote my past books, but going on a proper book tour across three cities was something altogether different. In every room and conversation, I could feel the anticipation and momentum behind the release of this book. There was a buzz in the air centered around this physical artifact that represented my best contribution to the world of personal development and inner work.

Here are my reflections on how it went and what I took away from it.

Los Angeles

First stop was Los Angeles, near where I grew up in Orange County. I hosted a book signing at The Last Bookstore, an ominously named shop that I felt alluded to the endangered state of reading in our attention-starved world.

The bookstore is in a repurposed bank, complete with a working vault packed with books, an amusing metaphor for knowledge as wealth. Towering columns, which I assume once conveyed trust and timeless authority, framed the main space where my event took place:

I had no idea how many people would show up for something like this, and was pleasantly surprised to greet around 25 attendees. About 7 of them were my family, and it was gratifying to be able to share this aspect of my work with them.

I had designed the agenda around one principle: What can we only do in person, not online?

I spent about 15 minutes talking about the book, what it was about, and how it came into existence. I explained how it connected to and addressed the gaps in my prior books. Then I led everyone through an embodied exercise demonstrating the book’s techniques in miniature form. Finally, I answered questions, and then signed books.

I’ve hosted a number of meetups in different cities before, and I’m always amazed at how people from my past will come out of the woodwork to meet me. At this event, a fellow Apple Store employee from when I worked there in college 18 years ago showed up, and we reminisced about our formative memories.

I met Azul Wells, who had taken my BASB course years ago and been inspired to start his own YouTube channel, which is now the leading channel on the subject of retirement with over 50 million views last year alone. I’m at a loss to even begin wrapping my head around the ripple effects of ideas I shared years ago that I think of as being in my rearview mirror.

The next day, we hosted the Annual Review Virtual Summit, welcoming several thousand attendees from all over the world to talk about the transformational impact of annual life reviews. I interviewed 10 guests chosen for their unique approach to structured reflection, and we all gleaned so many insights from what they shared.

As I set off for the next stop of my tour in San Francisco, my daughter gave me a small token of good luck – my book in miniature. A good reminder of how deeply the way I work influences my children, for whom it forms their model of what work is and means.

San Francisco

Flying to San Francisco felt like a homecoming in many ways, since most of the ideas I’ve written about and taught originated there.

Descending toward SFO airport, I gazed silently at my book lying on my fold-down table, thinking about everything that had happened to bring me to this moment – the failures, the heartbreak, the mistakes, the fear. I teared up, realizing that it was all the necessary groundwork to be able to create this system that so many people could now benefit from.

I recorded an interview with my friend Liz Moody for her podcast, and really enjoyed her witty and slightly irreverent take on the subject. As I talk to people outside my niche, I’m learning how universal reflective practice is, and yet how many different ways there are of understanding and practicing it.

I took BART to Powell St. station in the heart of downtown San Francisco, and as I was ascending the escalator to street level, I had a powerful wave of deja vu. I realized this was the exact elevator I’d used in March 2012, when I moved to the city to start my first job.

I was filled with the memories of uncertainty as well as excitement I felt at the time, striking out on my own in the big city to seek my fortune. In this picture I took at the time, I look like a kid:

Back then, I remember emerging out onto the bustling street on a beautiful sunny day, surrounded by tourists waiting for the trolleys that turn around on that spot. I emerged to find an identical scene greeting me this time as well.

I remember trudging up the street to the cheapest Airbnb room I could find. So cheap, in fact, that it had bedbugs, and I had to throw away most of my things almost as soon as I arrived.

I walked up the very same street toward Union Square, and was taken aback to notice my book through the glass, on display at The Best Bookstore where my signing would take place.

It told me I was known here, I was welcome here, and that there were people waiting to receive me this time. There I was again, 14 years later in the exact same spot, but now in such a different situation.

I checked in to my hotel and, a few hours later, headed back to the bookstore to start the event. Again, to my pleasant surprise, there were around 24 people who showed up, including some who I’d worked with on past books or courses.

I passed the microphone around and asked people where and how they’d encountered my work, and it ran the gamut from YouTube to my blog, from recent content I’d created on AI to some of my earliest writing on the Theory of Constraints. The crowd reflected the eclectic and sometimes meandering path I’d taken to get here.

I had a free day in San Francisco for the first time in a long time, and decided to go on a walk around town.

I visited the American Bookbinders Museum, which documented in fantastic detail the many, many innovations that took place across history in just one narrow aspect of bookmaking – the process of binding the pages.

Comparing the dirty, labor-intensive, error-prone process of the past with the totally seamless process of today, I felt grateful for all the obscure inventors who’d worked so hard to make one tiny step just slightly more efficient.

Visiting the SF Museum of Modern Art, I was struck repeatedly by prominent quotes on the walls that seemed highly relevant to the topic of my book, a reminder that any given work is part of a long lineage of thinking and feeling.

New York City

If San Francisco represented my past, and Los Angeles my present, then flying to New York felt like voyaging into the future. A wider horizon for where my ideas could lead me.

I did a book signing at Powerhouse Books on Columbus Circle, with around 26 people in attendance, with my friend Ryder Carroll as the moderator. Once again, they came from all over the region, from all walks of life, with such different relationships to me and my work.

The following days were filled with less public, but no less meaningful events. I attended an author’s dinner hosted by Alex & Books, where we talked for hours about our respective journeys through the publishing world.

I visited the 9/11 Memorial Museum and was amazed that such an extensive collection could be assembled to commemorate one single day in history. This quote from Virgil jumped out at me as a reminder that history can be created in a day, but not erased in a day.

I visited the offices of Simon & Schuster, my publisher, in Rockefeller Center for the first time. It felt like entering the inner sanctum of the literary world, towering above the streets of midtown Manhattan. My editor for this and the last two books, Stephanie, welcomed me.

We talked about the current and future state of publishing. I came away with the sense that they think on much longer timescales than the current worries around the supposed “death of reading.” People have worried about the decline of reading for centuries, but I think it’s doing just fine.

I walked through Times Square a couple of times, and as always was amazed by the buzzing proliferation of so many competing ideas, movies, Broadway shows, products, newscasts, and perspectives. They all compete on the level playing field of the Internet now, I realized, as do I. There are no commanding heights or privileged gatekeepers anymore, just a free-for-all on the global attention landscape.

I ended the trip with a visit to Bathhouse, a chic sauna in Williamsburg like something out of ancient Roman times, with my friend Ryder. The view of the Manhattan skyline from the rooftop pool was the perfect closing scene to a whirlwind trip.

The feeling I’m left with is that it all matters. It matters that writers spend years putting their best effort and thinking into books. It matters that people read those books and spend time immersed in new ways of seeing the world. The relationship between those two groups is one of the most precious parts of our culture in a world of increasingly fragmented attention, and I want to spend my career helping to strengthen it.

Most of all, I want to say an enormous THANK YOU to the hundreds of people who were part of creating and launching this book. Writing books is truly the furthest thing from a solo effort. It’s a community effort, and I’m immensely grateful to be part of such an interesting and supportive one. I’ll take that gratitude into my own annual review starting shortly!

And if you're ready to start building your Second Brain, get the book and learn the proven method to organize your digital life and unlock your creative potential.
