items.title: Big Time Off: The Transformative Power of Sabbaticals and How to Take One
items.summary: I recently shared that I’m starting to plan an epic multi-month road trip down the length of South America with my family, which I’m dubbing “ Operation Gallavant .” As I’ve begun digging into the details, it’s quickly become clear to me that the single biggest challenge isn’t…
items.author: Tiago Forte
items.contentHtml:
I recently shared that I’m starting to plan an epic multi-month road trip down the length of South America with my family, which I’m dubbing “Operation Gallavant.”

As I’ve begun digging into the details, it’s quickly become clear to me that the single biggest challenge isn’t going to be the travel logistics, homeschooling, or anything like that. It’s going to be taking months off work.

I know some long-term travelers work on the road, via Starlink or Internet cafes. But I knew right away that I didn’t want to do that. Having three young kids in tow makes it almost an impossibility, and besides, what’s the point of road-tripping if I’m just going to be stuck on my computer?

I want to be totally, 100% present during our South American overlanding trip, not even checking my emails on the margins or ruminating on my projects in the back of my mind. Which means that it’s slowly dawned on me that I’m going to be taking a sabbatical. That word snuck up on me, an implication unexpectedly popping out of my other plans.

It was serendipitous that, just as I was considering all this, a new book appeared on my desk addressing exactly this topic: Big Time Off, by DJ DiDonna.

It’s the culmination of years of work by an organization he founded called The Sabbatical Project, which aims to spread awareness and acceptance of sabbaticals as an essential part of modern work life.

I read the book with an eye toward my own future sabbatical, and here’s what I learned that has made the biggest difference for me.

The research

One of the first things DiDonna discovered as he set out to understand sabbaticals was that little research existed on the topic. He had to conduct his own.

Through a series of studies, he found that sabbaticals alleviated burnout, increased creativity, improved relationships, and helped people reinvent themselves. Remarkably, the people he studied described their sabbaticals as “peak life experiences” on par with their wedding day or the birth of a child.

The language that kept arising in his research was that taking several months off of work allowed them to “feel human again.” The day-to-day work routine has a tendency to inflict a continuous storm of “slings and arrows” on our psyche. Perhaps none of them deal a crippling blow, but the gradual accumulation weighs on our soul.

Sabbaticals are a way to unburden it.

In his research, DiDonna found that only about 50% of couples who are fifty today can expect both partners to be mentally and physically able to travel extensively by the time they reach retirement age. That’s an astonishing finding when the standard attitude is “we’ll travel when we’re retired.”

The single best predictor of a person’s likelihood of taking a sabbatical is whether they know someone who has taken one. Thus, Big Time Off is full of stories of real people who took the plunge. These stories are some of the most potent raw material to begin constructing your own version of what it could look like.

Most of these stories weren’t from people who were in crisis. But they also didn’t possess so-called “post-economic” wealth. They were mid-career, with both successes and failures under their belt, and often with kids. They had to draw most of all on their creativity and imagination to carve out the sabbatical months.

This was perhaps my biggest takeaway from the book: that a sabbatical doesn’t have to be a shining mountain that you reach “one day,” when you’ve figured everything out and achieved all your goals. It is a project like any other, and you can make it happen much earlier with some ingenuity.

The origins

The word “sabbatical” comes from the old Hebrew šabbat, or Sabbath, referring to the weekly day of rest deeply ingrained in Jewish culture. You can think of a sabbatical as a Sabbath not for a week, but for a much longer timescale of years.

The first official sabbatical policy was created at Harvard in 1879 for the purpose of “health, rest, study, or the prosecution of original work in literature or science.” This extended break from their usual teaching duties was essential to allow academics to collaborate with their European counterparts, who tended to take summers off.

After experimenting with different periods of time off, Harvard settled on a full year of paid leave, which has remained the norm today, 150 years later. Within 40 years of its creation, fifty top universities had adopted similar policies. From academia, the practice slowly started spreading to the corporate and governmental sectors.

Fast forward to today, sabbaticals are becoming an increasingly common and accepted life stage. The number of American employees who are on sabbatical at any given time has tripled in just the last five years according to The Sabbatical Project’s surveys. Younger workers are twice as likely to take a sabbatical as older generations. Hiring managers are beginning to view it as a positive life choice and a sign of lifelong learning and growth.

Why take a sabbatical

DiDonna spends much of his book persuading the reader to take the possibility of a sabbatical seriously, even if it seems out of reach.

He notes that we tend only to take extended leave when it’s forced on us – in the form of a health emergency, being laid off unexpectedly, or during a downturn in our industry or the economy. But this approach is like waiting to go to the dentist until you need a root canal. Much better to do regular cleanings.

A sabbatical is an intentional process of planning, saving up, and making space for a break on your own schedule, on your own terms, to serve the purpose of your own choosing. It’s the act of pushing back against the incessant demands for productivity and progress and prioritizing your long-term personal growth instead.

Two of the most cited changes among sabbatical takers are increases in perspective and confidence. What could be more important for you to gain more of mid-career, when facing some of the most consequential, high-stakes decisions that will shape the latter half of your working years?

A sabbatical is a gift you give yourself. The gift of stepping back to see your life clearly, from a wider longer-term perspective, while you still have time to make major changes. It’s the rejection of your professional identity as the only identity that matters.

DiDonna recommends taking at least 6 months off for a sabbatical, which represents a little more than 1% of the typical 40-year career. I think it’s a small price to pay to align the remaining 99%.

Functional workaholism

I was struck by DiDonna’s definition of “functional workaholism,” which he said was a common condition that led people to take a sabbatical. He described it as “an ongoing state of gradually deteriorating job engagement, efficacy, and personal health.”

This is different from burnout. It’s the slowly accumulating background stress that, if left unchecked, eventually leads to burnout.

He tells the heart-wrenching story of a high-achieving law partner whose firm offered sabbatical policies:

“He and his son had always dreamed of hiking part of the Appalachian Trail together, but when his son graduated high school, the father was close enough to a major promotion that he skipped his sabbatical. Four years later, he’d achieved his career goals, but his son was too busy starting his first job out of college to join the hike. It wasn’t an acute tragedy, but it was a pretty big missed opportunity.”

I see myself in these portraits of the functional workaholic so clearly.

On the surface, everything looks fine, or even great. I work reasonable hours, on projects of my choosing, with broad autonomy, and make great money. I spend lots of time with my family, friends, and on exercise and hobbies.

This would be an enviable position for many, and I’m not complaining.

But there are small signs: the compulsion to work on weekends and on vacation, not because I have to, but because it’s when I feel most alive and engaged. It’s the coping mechanisms of caffeine, sugar, and social media I find myself turning to to eke out a little more productivity from an aching body. It’s the moments playing with my kids when my mind is elsewhere, or I feel too tired to give them the attention they need.

None of this is anywhere close to an emergency. I could easily keep going this way forever. No one would notice anything amiss, and many would even admire me for this relatively laid-back lifestyle. But there is another state I’m looking for, that I’ve occasionally tasted: when my work doesn’t always get the best of me.

This has made me realize that I’m scared of the boredom, the lack of feeling useful, and the absence of visible progress that stepping back from work will entail. But I’m also curious to know: who am I apart from the role I’ve played as an entrepreneur, founder, and CEO?

The opportunity for the business

Besides changing my personal relationship with my work, the other big opportunity I see is to reshape the nature of my business.

I started my career enamored with the ideas of Rich Dad, Poor Dad, the promise of “passive” income, and the siren song of “evergreen” information products that could be sold while I slept. I saw the hard-grinding careers of older generations and wanted nothing to do with them.

But over time, the idea of letting systems do work on my behalf faded into the background. The pandemic exploded our revenue and opportunities, and it felt only natural to chase those opportunities with everything I had.

The last 6 years have flashed by, and it feels like that whole time I’ve been in “wartime mode,” pushing and striving and maximizing growth, when my essential nature is more that of a wandering artist.

I see a chance to redesign Forte Labs in such a way that it can withstand my absence, and thus justify starting to wander again. And I know that won’t happen until I’m truly absent for a long stretch. I’ll need to invest a lot more authority and autonomy in the team, redesign our educational programs to not rely on me as the sole instructor, and focus more on existing products that can be incrementally improved, whereas I tend to favor wholesale new creations.

One of the most intriguing aspects of the book was that DiDonna doesn’t recommend necessarily abstaining from all forms of work during a sabbatical. The goal is not to sit on a beach sipping from a coconut the entire time. That could be maddeningly boring, especially for those who enjoy thinking, learning, and efforting.

Instead, the intention is to do a different kind of work than you’re normally used to. To break the usual pattern, and thus explore a new aspect of your identity or develop a new interest. That could be building a deck if you normally work at a computer all day. Or taking a class and becoming a student in a new field. Or dedicating oneself to a community service project or important cause.

Without a boss evaluating your performance, or a fixed set of responsibilities to uphold, or the demands of company politics, you’re free to redefine your relationship to work as something intrinsic and freely chosen, not just an obligation.

DiDonna writes: “…until you’ve left your life behind, you cannot truly change; you’re stuck with a foot in the old world. If you’re going to take a journey, commit.”

In a company setting, taking a sabbatical is a helpful opportunity to reveal the full scope of an employee’s responsibilities. Rather than their work piling up on their desk or in their inbox until they get back, that work has to be transferred to others. That provides a chance to unpack what’s necessary and what’s not, and to develop resilience toward turnover.

I’ve always known that I am the bottleneck to the company’s growth, and my sabbatical will give me a chance to test what it would look like to remove it.

Three archetypes

DiDonna describes three archetypes of people who take sabbaticals. Many tend to be a mix of more than one.

The Achiever views their sabbatical first and foremost as an achievement; that is, an opportunity to get things done. They often use external markers – like mastering a new language, writing a book, or completing a long trek – to mark their progress. The pitfall is that they can use these projects to avoid looking inside and examining their true desires. If this is you, the greatest use of a sabbatical might be to take a break from this mindset itself.

The Seeker is someone who grapples with uncertainty and often goes on a journey of some kind to resolve it: either physically, like traveling to see friends or family or inspiring places, or spiritually, voyaging into their inner world. Seekers set out to find answers to their most deeply held questions. Their pitfall is that they can hold unrealistic expectations about the depth of the transformation they experience.

The Explorer mainly wants to find out what’s out there in the world, and is less concerned with the practical application of what they find. This may involve time away from home, backpacking or road-tripping, or exploring a stack of books. Their intention is to widen the aperture on what’s possible. The potential pitfall could be that their sabbatical lacks intention and focus.

Protean careers

The rise of sabbaticals has coincided with a shift in the nature of modern careers. DiDonna dubs it the “Protean career,” because it’s no longer enough to climb a predefined ladder step by step – you now have to regularly reinvent and reimagine your career, much like Proteus, the shape-shifting sea god of Greek mythology.

Lifespans are also getting longer, and therefore, so are career spans. Our forties and fifties are no longer the twilight of our working lives; they may be only a halfway mark with decades left to come. That means more chances to pivot toward a new role, or even a whole new career.

Many of our careers are now entrepreneurial by necessity, which demands a deeper, more creative approach. We alone are in charge of our direction, our choices, and the fulfillment (or lack thereof) that we derive from our work. The playing field of possible options is vaster than ever, and the landscape is more uncertain and quickly changing than any previous generation knew.

A sabbatical can be understood as a strategic rehearsal and insurance plan to step back and redirect your career strategically, instead of waiting for it to be forced upon you. It’s less about specific skill acquisition and more about gaining the perspective and courage you’ll need to face the future proactively.

The connection to annual life reviews

While reading Big Time Off, I was struck by the many parallels to my own teaching on annual life reviews, as recounted in my new book Life in Perspective.

DiDonna writes:

“Living in alignment requires recurring adjustments over the course of your life, informed by who you are, how you’ve changed since the last time you checked, and clarity about who you want to be.”

I couldn’t agree more! In a way, I think an annual life review is a mini version of a sabbatical, geared toward many of the same intentions but occurring on a 12-month rhythm.

I see many ways these two structures can be complementary – the annual review gives you a pre-scheduled time to revisit and reflect on the year, while the sabbatical is its heavier-duty cousin for when you need to step back even further, and take even more time, to dig into the depths of your identity.

Both rituals are a chance to intentionally answer the question, “Who am I, apart from the roles I’ve played?”

The post Big Time Off: The Transformative Power of Sabbaticals and How to Take One appeared first on Forte Labs.

items.title: 😺 DeepMind's new AI exam
items.author: Corey Noles
items.contentHtml:
SHARE
Add The Neuron as a preferred source

😺 DeepMind's new AI exam

Written By
Corey Noles
Co-Authors
Corey Noles
Eric Gerard Ruiz
Corey Noles
Nov 25, 2026
· 8 minute read

Welcome, humans.

So apparently Google told every AI agent that wants into your Gmail to use the front door from now on. Google made its Workspace MCP servers and command-line tool generally available, and starting February 1, 2027, agents must reach Workspace data through them instead of calling Google's regular APIs directly.

Translation. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is a standard plug that lets an AI agent talk to an app, and these servers cover Gmail, Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Calendar, Chat, and Tasks. Going through that door lets admins see what each agent does, require a human thumbs-up for risky actions, and keep an audit log. Google's post doesn't say how it will enforce the deadline.

Your inbox finally has a bouncer, and the bouncer keeps receipts.

Here’s what happened in AI today:

  • 😸 DeepMind launched a test for consistent AI answers

  • 📰 Anthropic and OpenAI staff doubt unreleased models are safe

  • 📰 OpenAI's GPT-6.2 designed lab-tested protein binders

  • 🍪 Claude artifacts now install as desktop apps

  • 🧠 GPT-6.2 Astra identified an 1808 sketchbook's artist

... and a whole lot more that you can read about here.

😸 DeepMind built an exam that checks if AI gets easy questions right every time

Google DeepMind launched Humanity's First Exam, a test of 544 everyday questions for AI models. The name winks at Humanity's Last Exam, a famously brutal benchmark (a standardized test for AI). This one goes the other direction.

Instead of asking whether a model can crack one impossible problem, it asks whether the model gets an easy problem right every time. The test checks each task plus slight variations of it. Think of the coworker who nails a spreadsheet on Monday and fumbles the same one on Tuesday. Smart, sure. Reliable, no.

Here's a sample. One prompt shows a neon sign and asks for the color of the third letter in each word, separated by semicolons. The correct answer is green; yellow; white; blue; blue. You could do that in seconds. Doing it correctly across every tweaked version is the actual test.

Here's what's in it:

  • 544 prompts covering text and images, grouped into sets of four related questions across 20 foundational capabilities

  • Tasks like counting objects, naming colors and symbols, tracking positions, basic arithmetic, following strict formatting, and spotting false premises (a trick question built on something untrue)

  • A live leaderboard on Kaggle (a site where data scientists compete and share datasets)

  • A three-week Kaggle contest through December 15, where anyone can submit everyday questions that current models still get wrong

DeepMind says frontier models made significant progress on the exam over the last six months, but the scoring is harsh. A model has to get all four versions of a question right, and one slip across 16 tries fails the whole set. Reported launch scores on that strict test put OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra first at 90.7%, then GPT-6.2 Sol at 87.5% and Gemini 4 Neon at 85.6%. On a single try, top models reach roughly 95% to 98%. Easy questions, and the best score is still barely an A-minus.

Our take: Simple here means the stuff a kid can do without thinking. Counting the objects in a photo, naming a color, tracking where something moved, adding two numbers, following an exact format, or catching a trick question built on something untrue. Those skills sit inside nearly every everyday request, like asking AI to total a receipt from a photo.

That's why this exam matters for the casual user. They ask quick questions, trust the answer, and rarely double-check. A model that aces expert math but miscounts the items on a shelf will burn them the moment they stop paying attention. DeepMind's technical report reportedly traced 73% of wrong answers to visual perception, so photo questions are the soft spot. The contest through December 15 invites people to submit the everyday questions models still miss.

FROM OUR PARTNERS

Wispr Flow Notetaker is now on iPhone

Record in-person conversations and get a clean summary and transcript afterward. Notetaker keeps recording even with your phone locked.

Get it on iPhone

🎓 AI Skill of the Day: Make your own call before the AI does

Ever notice how a polished AI answer turns into your answer by the time you finish reading it? Researchers Hüseyin Hussein Keke, Daniel Eisenhardt, and Christian Meske tested a fix in a study of 130 people solving problems. Some people committed to their own answer first and only then saw the AI's input.

That group made better decisions than people who got AI help right away or no AI help at all. They also used the AI's prompts more. The idea is that a mismatch between your answer and the AI's forces a second, slower look. Disagreement is annoying. Annoying is useful. It's one experiment, so treat it as a promising nudge and not a law.

Here's our adaptation for a low-stakes decision:

  1. Write your answer and one reason in a notes app before you open the chat.

  2. Ask the AI for its own recommendation, without sharing yours.

  3. Wherever the two differ, paste in yours and ask for the strongest case against it. 

Here is my call and my reason: [your answer + reason]. Make the strongest case against it, then list the facts I should verify before I decide.

Have a specific skill you want to learn? Request it here.

FROM OUR PARTNERS

Attio is the #1 fastest-growing CRM on Brex and Ramp.

Built for the most ambitious companies in GTM, Attio is an end to end revenue platform that allows teams to run multiple plays across different revenue motions and lifecycles.

Teams at the frontier are already building on it: Granola, turbopuffer, Modal, and many many more.

Start building on Attio.

📰 Around the Horn

Stefan 3D AI says $6,528 worth of Claude Fable 5.2 tokens built this entire fantasy RPG in one week. Five races, 16 quests, and six mounts you can glide around on. $6,528 sounds like a lot until you remember a game like this normally takes a studio months and a payroll.

  • Axios reported that more than two dozen sources say many Anthropic and OpenAI staff doubt their strongest unreleased models can ship safely, though nothing is decided.

  • OpenAI reported in a preprint that GPT-6.2 designed protein shapes, and 35 of 322 tested candidates bound their targets in lab tests, though specialized tools helped filter them.

  • At least 42 states and D.C. challenged Character.AI's bankruptcy auction, which would sell chat histories from more than 21M U.S. accounts, including 2.1M belonging to minors.

  • Axios reported that security experts expect rushed patching of AI-discovered bugs to raise the risk of service outages.

  • Google's Threat Intelligence Group reported its first sighting of attackers using AI to both find and exploit software flaws with no human involved.

  • The volunteer Leonida project, which used AI coding tools to port leaked GTA 6 code to PC, lost its GitHub page and Discord servers, though the cause is unconfirmed.

Want absolutely EVERYTHING that happened in AI this week? Click here!

🍪 Treats to Try

*Asterisk = from our partners (only the first one!). Advertise to 700K+ readers here!

  1. Why Successful AI Pilots Still Struggle to Reach Enterprise Scale. Read more

  2. Google Workspace's MCP servers and CLI are now generally available, so your agents can reach Gmail, Drive, Docs, Sheets, Calendar, and more through one managed connection.

  3. Claude artifacts now install as Mac and Windows desktop apps, so a tool you built in chat gets its own icon and window (beta, and Enterprise owners must enable it).

  4. Meta's Muse opened to UK adults 18 and over, where it can shop at Currys, book Trainline or easyJet trips, and asks before it buys anything.

  5. Baidu's ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview released downloadable weights under an Apache 2.0 license, so you can run a 1M-token-context model yourself, though Baidu calls it an unfinished checkpoint.

  6. SenseNova U1.6 is an open 8B image model that checks its own picture against your prompt and redraws garbled or misspelled text.

  7. Cognition's SWE-2.1 is the new default coding model in Devin Desktop, Cloud, and CLI, and Cognition says it scores 50.0% on Terminal-Bench 4.1, up from 24.2%.

  8. Fleetify is an open-source desktop app that runs several coding agents side by side, each in its own git worktree so their changes never collide.

  9. Almma's PII Guard is a Chrome extension that flags names, emails, and ID numbers in your Claude chat box before you hit send, then swaps in placeholders.

🧠 Midweek Wisdom

  • Mark Humphries showed that GPT-6.2 Astra ruled out both artists he suggested for an 1808 sketchbook and found the real one, but he still ordered the journals to confirm it by handwriting. AI can fix your wrong starting assumption, which is a real gift, but it hands you a lead, not a verdict, so check the proof before you repeat it.

  • Fabrizio Dell'Acqua and coauthors found in a P&G experiment that AI improved ideas but not the choosing, as teams picked their best idea about 37% of the time versus roughly 50% without it. More good options make picking harder, so slow down at the choosing step, because that part is still your job.

  • Anthropic's Erik Schluntz and Barry Zhang wrote that many tasks need only one well-prompted AI call, because agents trade speed and cost for performance, so add complexity only when it pays off. That applies to anyone's AI setup, not only developers, so try one good prompt before you build a fancy multi-step workflow.

New from The Neuron: AI Explained

New episodes air every week on Wednesdays: | Apple Podcasts | YouTube

A Cat’s Commentary

That’s all for now. If you want to get featured above, fill out the poll below and tell us how we did today!

What'd you think of today's email?

  • 🐾🐾🐾🐾🐾 Like a hit of catnip
  • 🐾🐾🐾 Good, not great
  • 🐾 It sucked

Corey Noles
Managing Editor

Corey Noles is the Managing Editor of the Sales, Business Intelligence, and IT blogs on TechnologyAdvice.com. He comes to TA with more than 20 years of experience in journalism and publishing, running newsrooms, planning content, chasing beats, and hiring great writers. Throughout his career, Corey has covered all aspects of technology, including artificial intelligence, space, business tech, consumer tech, IoT, and much more. In recent months, Corey has begun taking courses in artificial intelligence, Generative AI prompt engineering, AI applications for business, AI strategy for business, machine learning, and applying artificial intelligence in python programming.

items.title: Voyager’s cosmic map of Earth’s location: Cute, but wrong
items.summary: Here in late 2026, an incredible milestone has been reached: the Voyager 1 spacecraft — humanity’s most distant spacecraft from Earth — has finally passed a distance of one light-day from us. Along with its twin, Voyager 2, these two spacecraft have left the confines of the…
items.author: Ethan Siegel
items.contentHtml:
Here in late 2026, an incredible milestone has been reached: the Voyager 1 spacecraft — humanity’s most distant spacecraft from Earth — has finally passed a distance of one light-day from us. Along with its twin, Voyager 2, these two spacecraft have left the confines of the Solar System and now traverse interstellar space, freely floating through the interstellar medium. Eventually, their radioactive sources will decay away enough that they’ll become entirely inoperable, but there’s a chance that someday, in the far future, an alien species will encounter and recover one or both of these ancient artifacts: humanity’s first foray into the Universe beyond our own Solar System.

Aboard each of these two Voyagers is a special message intended for anyone who’d find them, whether in the near or distant future: the Voyager golden record. Containing songs, images, and sounds of Earth, it was designed to be an information-laden cosmic time capsule, capable of being easily deciphered by any intelligent alien species to come upon it. It was meant as an introduction to Earth and humanity, with the vision of serving as a cultural ambassador for our planet.

Emblazoned on the cover of the record are a series of diagrams, including one that we thought was incredibly important at the time: a map of Earth’s location in the galaxy, as determined through the mapping of 14 radio-loud pulsars. Although the method used to locate Earth was, for its time, a very clever one, we now understand that it’s inherently flawed. Anyone who receives it will most likely be unable to track down where our planet is from the included information, making it a cute, but wrongheaded, artifact from our cosmic infancy.

The whole point of the golden record was that it would serve as sort of a “time capsule” of humanity and Earth: an attempt to reach out to whomever might be out there in the Universe and share with them a little bit about what our world is like and what humanity — at its best — is all about. Carl Sagan, cocreator of the golden record, put it as follows:

“We [are] a species endowed with hope and perseverance, at least a little intelligence, substantial generosity and a palpable zest to make contact with the cosmos.”

Today, despite our stumbles and missteps in the 49 years that have ensued since the launch of the dual Voyager spacecraft, all of these things remain true.

At the time, pulsars were a relatively new discovery. The very first one had only been discovered back in 1967, when then-graduate student Jocelyn Bell (later Jocelyn Bell Burnell), while surveying the sky for quasars, instead found a surprising signal on her chart-recorder papers that she described as a “bit of scruff.” After digging into that signal, she found that it was a radio emitter that pulsed with great regularity. Initially named LGM-1, for “Little Green Man 1,” it was soon determined not to be a signal of alien origin at all, but rather a rapidly rotating neutron star that emitted radio pulses. Today, that neutron star is known as our first pulsar, and has the less-poetic name PSR B1919+21.

Bell Burnell herself was the one who showed that this was unlikely to be a signal from intelligent extraterrestrials, when she continued her work and found a similar signal originating from a different part of the sky. Thomas Gold suggested the origin of pulsars should be rapidly rotating neutron stars the year after they were first discovered, in 1968. Originally discovered in the radio band, pulsars were swiftly detected over a wide variety of wavelengths across the electromagnetic spectrum. The first optical pulsar was discovered in January of 1969, and in May of 1969 the first X-ray pulsar was discovered in the heart of the Crab Nebula: a pulsar that was known to emit radio waves since the year prior.

By the time the Voyager spacecraft were launched in 1977, there were a cumulative 149 pulsars that had been discovered, and pulsar evolution had also been detected. In late 1968, the Crab pulsar’s period was found to slowly increase, meaning that the pulsar was spinning down over time. In 1969, the first “glitch” in a pulsar system was detected: an instantaneous change in the pulse period of a pulsar. Pulse period decay was identified in many more pulsars, and as of 1977, the period of the known pulsars ranged from a little over 1 second to as fast as 33 pulses per second.

We also had a rudimentary picture — just ten years after their initial discovery — for how these pulsars worked. The idea was that a neutron star was spinning, and that a neutron star itself isn’t just a ball of neutrons, but rather is a core of dense neutrons surrounded by a thin shell of atomic nuclei, including a mix of protons and neutrons combined, and much lighter electrons as well. As the neutron star spins, the much heavier protons and the much lighter electrons separate, and wind up with slightly different distributions across the neutron star’s outer layers and surface.

Whenever you have a set of electric charges in motion, they’re going to produce a magnetic field. The more charges you have, the greater a charge separation you have, the greater the charge density you have, and the faster the charges move, the stronger the generated magnetic field will be. Whereas the Earth has a magnetic field of about 1 Gauss, the strongest permanent magnets we can generate have a field strength of around 14,000 Gauss, and the strongest laboratory electromagnets have a magnitude of around 300,000-500,000 Gauss, the strength of a rotating neutron star’s magnetic field can routinely reach or exceed 100 trillion Gauss (10 Gauss): incredibly strong magnetic fields.

The idea is that these fields then accelerate material, such as electrons, around them, and the accelerated material produces “blips” of radiation each time the pulsar completes one revolution.

With this picture in mind, it made a lot of sense to choose several among the known pulsars and map the Earth’s location relative to them, with the relative distance to each of those pulsars noted in the diagram. This “pulsar map” of our location was an attempt to create a reference frame that an extraterrestrial species would instantly be able to recognize. Sure, there were other choices we could have made, but they’d all have drawbacks.

  • We could have shown aliens our night sky, but the relative positions of stars in the sky change swiftly: over thousands of years. Voyager’s map would no longer look like our skies by the time anyone received them.
  • We could have mapped out the intrinsically brightest, more distant stars, but the brightest ones are the shortest-lived, and so there’s a good chance that many of them would no longer be present by the time anyone received them.
  • We could have mapped out our position relative to the galactic center or the nearest spiral arm, but we both rotate around the galaxy and drift relative to the arm-and-spur features within our galaxy; such a map would have made it difficult for an alien species to reconstruct where we actually are now by the time we received such a message.

At the time, it made sense to go with a map of pulsars: a new species of regularly beating stellar remnants that remain at a relatively large, constant distance from us (at least over hundred thousand-to-million year timescales), and whose pulse frequency would only change by small amounts over time. In theory, these pulsars could have remained relatively stable for up to tens of millions of years.

The pulsars that were chosen were chosen judiciously. First, there were 14 of them that were selected: all pulsars that were among the most regular and slowest-decaying of the known ones at the time. Second, they came in a variety of distances and from a variety of directions: close to the galactic center, on the opposite side of the sky from the galactic center, across the plane of the Milky Way, and some even in the galactic halo, with distances ranging from just a few thousand light-years away to many tens-of-thousands of light-years away. And third, their pulse period was encoded into the diagram, along with the directions and relative distances of those pulsars.

The idea was that anyone, even after millions of years, who found the map would be able to identify those same pulsars, figure out what star they were pointing to, and would be pointed in the direction of our Sun and Solar System. That was the intent of the pulsar map.

Unfortunately, now that we live here in 2026 instead of 1977, we know that there’s an enormous amount that’s wrong with sending our pulsar map to aliens and expecting that they’d be able to identify where we are based on the information encoded in that map. Here are the biggest flaws with the information we provided.

1.) Pulsars, and neutron stars in general, are far more common and numerous than anyone realized back in 1977.

There are approximately 400 billion stars in the Milky Way itself, and about 1 in 800 out of all the stars that are ever born are massive enough that they’ll ultimately die in a core-collapse supernova. While a small fraction of those will produce black holes, the overwhelming majority instead result in the production of neutron stars. That means there are likely between 400 and 500 million neutron stars in the Milky Way today that have arisen from these stellar remnants, and around 50 to 100 million of those will be pulsars for somebody, depending on their line-of-sight.

Rather than providing a map of rare objects that can be identified by anyone, we’ve given a map of fourteen particular pieces of hay within an enormous haystack. Only, there are only around 1-to-4 million pieces of hay in an actual haystack, versus more than an order of magnitude more pulsars in our actual Milky Way. Given that the periods of these pulsars are changing, and that these particular pulsars are the types that are prone to glitches, it’s unlikely that someone finding our map will be able to even identify which pulsars we were intending to indicate on the map itself.

2.) Pulsars don’t emit their pulses omnidirectionally, but only along a particular line-of-sight, so what appears to pulse for one observer doesn’t pulse for everyone.

We used to not know this, but pulsars don’t appear to pulse for everyone. A pulsar has a magnetic field in a similar fashion to how a planet like Earth has a magnetic field: with two main “poles” to it where magnetic fields lines enter and leave the surface of the stellar remnant. As the neutron star rotates, these two poles sweep around and accelerate particles within them, generating electromagnetic waves — or forms of light, including radio light — that can be perceived as pulses by anyone who’s lucky enough to receive them.

But we only exist in one location in spacetime, so we only receive a series of pulses from the select few pulsars that happen to be lined up with us. Any observer in a different location is unlikely to see the same pulsars that we do; they will have a different set of neutron stars that appear to pulse for them, and given that we may only be seeing fewer than 1-in-10,000 actual pulsars at any given time, it’s possible that anyone who picks up Voyager 1 or 2 won’t even recognize a single one of the pulsars that we’re pointing out.

3.) Pulsars precess over time, so that pulsars don’t appear to “pulse” for the same observer indefinitely, and instead turn on and turn off for observers over time.

This one is an even trickier part of the problem: many pulsars have binary companions, in the form of stars, black holes, planets, other neutron stars, or white dwarfs. The gravitational influence of a companion can cause the plane of the pulsar’s orbit, as well as the plane of the pulsar’s rotation, to change over time. That means that pulsars that “pulse” for us today may rotate out of our line-of-sight in the future (some have already done this), whereas pulsars that are currently out of our line-of-sight may someday rotate into it.

This makes it exceedingly unlikely that even just a million years from now, the same set of pulsars will be pulsing from the perspective of an observer on Earth, or for any observer at any location in the Universe. As pulsars turn on-and-off, their intrinsic properties like their period or their magnetic field aren’t necessarily changing, but rather their orientation of where they point gradually changes over time. As such, these pulsars included on the pulsar map very likely will no longer be pointing at Earth by the time someone receives them. In fact, it’s eminently likely that not a single one of them will still be pointing at us.

4.) As pulsars evolve over time, they turn off; most older neutron stars go quiet due to either a reduction in their magnetic field or a spin-down in their rate of rotation.

And finally, not all neutron stars are thought to be pulsars at all. It’s thought that a neutron star needs to be a combination of a fast enough rotator and to possess a strong enough magnetic field in order for it to pulse at all. Although there are slow pulsars, they are all thought to have powerful magnetic fields, and a powerful magnetic field on its own is not a guarantee that you’ll get a pulsar, as some strongly magnetized neutron stars become magnetars instead. As neutron stars evolve, they tend to spin down and slow their rotation, and their magnetic fields can also weaken with time. Therefore, the neutron stars that are pulsing today may not necessarily continue pulsing far into the future.

The timescale for this can be long: up to hundreds of millions of years for the longest-lived pulsars. However, because they weren’t known in 1977, none of the 14 pulsars included on the Voyager golden records are this long-lived species of pulsar at all! It’s again quite likely that after just millions of years, or perhaps even a shorter period of time, these pulsars will turn off and cease pulsing entirely: not just for us, but for everyone. This map, therefore, represents a mere snapshot of what was pulsing and pointing at us back in 1977. Decades, centuries, millennia, or aeons from now, that will not necessarily be the case any longer.

When the Voyager spacecraft launched, we had only known about pulsars for a decade; they were brand new, exciting, and represented the cutting edge of what we knew about in the field of astronomy. But in the here and now, more than a quarter of the way through the 21st century, we know that there are better, rarer objects out there.

  • A sub-class of pulsars, millisecond pulsars, were only first discovered in 1982: pulsars that are much more stable and are much faster rotators.
  • There are binary pulsars, or systems where a pulsar and another neutron star orbit one another, with predictable inspiral timetables that can be detected via sensitive enough gravitational wave detectors, rather than needing to be along a pulsar’s line-of-sight.
  • And instead of 149 known pulsars, our pulsar counts have increased over time: to 558 in the 1993 catalogue, to 1297 in the 2003 catalogue, to 2267 in the 2013 catalogue, to 3473 in the 2024 catalogue and, in real time at the ATNF pulsar catalogue, up to 4503 today.

The study of pulsar evolution through timing, through glitches, and through pulse profile changes have all greatly advanced our understanding of these objects. They’ve taught us that someone receiving Voyager’s pulsar map would likely think it was a cute attempt at a map the way an adult viewing a child’s drawing of their house relative to Earth might find it cute, rather than fulfilling the desire that Frank Drake expressed about the pulsar map itself.

“We needed to put something on the Voyager that said where it came from, and how long it was traveling… There was a magic about pulsars … no other things in the sky had such labels on them. Each one had its own distinct pulsing frequency, so it could be identified by anybody, including other creatures after a long period of time and far, far away.”

Of course, its lack of utility also rules out the interpretation that we sent out a dangerous map that will lead to our own destruction. The truth is sobering and humbling: what appears to be the cutting edge of science to us, in the here-and-now, may indeed be something we look back on in a generation or two as an incredibly naive perspective on reality. This is not a flaw, however; it is a feature of science. As our knowledge and capabilities improve, it is a call for us to redouble our commitment to understanding, exploring, and striving for new frontiers in the cosmos.

This article Voyager’s cosmic map of Earth’s location: Cute, but wrong is featured on Big Think.

items.title: Macy’s T-Day Parade might be without balloons
items.summary: Manoli Figetakis/Getty Images When your family tunes into the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade tomorrow, the mood might be less than buoyant. The 100th edition of the Big Apple event may have to proceed without the iconic balloons as a storm is expected to lash the East Coast…
items.author: Sam Klebanov
items.contentHtml:
When your family tunes into the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade tomorrow, the mood might be less than buoyant. The 100th edition of the Big Apple event may have to proceed without the iconic balloons as a storm is expected to lash the East Coast from Delaware to Long Island.

On top of rain, forecasters warn of 35-mph winds with gusts of up to 60 mph starting at 10am in New York City and continuing throughout Turkey Day. Balloons can’t fly if sustained winds hit 23 mph and gusts reach 34 mph, according to city rules meant to protect spectators from injury.

Balloon bummer?

Macy’s said the decision whether to float Snoopy, Mickey, and friends will be made tomorrow morning before the event starts at 8:30am.

Officials warn that balloons might have to be deflated on side streets off the parade route, which runs until noon(ish) through Manhattan’s streets, where skyscrapers often create wind tunnels.

What might we miss out on?

  • This year’s parade is slated to feature over 100 inflatables, as opposed to the usual 50–60.
  • Bluey and Sorcerer’s Apprentice Mickey are among the new balloons.

Float first-timers include a tribute to the puppeteer Tony Sarg who created the event’s first “reverse-marionettes” in 1928 and an HBO-sponsored display for its forthcoming Harry Potter series.

Outside Manhattan: East Coast winds could also impact travel of those who plan to fly tomorrow, while California drivers might have to deal with coastal flooding from king tides.—SK

items.title: Tidal is first major streaming service to ban AI music
items.summary: Nick Iluzada If you’re looking for the latest song from Tilly Norwood, you’ll soon have to find it somewhere other than Tidal. Starting on Dec. 9, Tidal will become the first major music streaming platform to ban tracks it believes are completely AI-generated. Tidal is going…
items.author: Dave Lozo
items.contentHtml:
If you’re looking for the latest song from Tilly Norwood, you’ll soon have to find it somewhere other than Tidal. Starting on Dec. 9, Tidal will become the first major music streaming platform to ban tracks it believes are completely AI-generated.

Tidal is going beyond the measures that rivals like Spotify and Apple Music have implemented to combat audio slop, which include labeling it while still allowing users to listen. Tidal’s stronger repudiation will result in the removal of 29 million songs. It also said that 43% of tracks distributed to the platform in the past 90 days have been detected as AI-generated.

While this news is sure to upset a guy in San Francisco who has developed a parasocial relationship with Tilly, a recent survey from the streaming service Deezer found that ~41% of Americans want 100% of AI-generated music screened out from their listening experience (Deezer is rolling out a toggle to filter out AI music).

Meanwhile, musicians have sued record labels Universal and Warner for allegedly licensing their songs for AI training without permission. Goldman Sachs predicts that labels will boost their revenue by 10% by 2035 through AI-related licensing opportunities.—DL

items.title: Trump admin. to unveil new tariffs any day now
items.summary: Morning Brew Inc., Photo: Allen J. Schaben/Getty Images Another one: The US is set to announce a new plan to hike levies on products from China, the EU, and 14 other nations that the Trump administration accuses of supporting their own domestic manufacturing to America’s…
items.author: Molly Liebergall
items.contentHtml:
Another one: The US is set to announce a new plan to hike levies on products from China, the EU, and 14 other nations that the Trump administration accuses of supporting their own domestic manufacturing to America’s detriment, the Wall Street Journal reported yesterday.

The rates of the new, country-specific duties aren’t yet clear, but:

  • They’ll apply to most products exported by the affected nations. Industrial goods that are tariffed separately, like cars and steel, will likely be excluded, per WSJ.
  • The new tariffs will be added to existing levies, but overall rates won’t surpass the caps that trading partners negotiated with Trump over the past year, Bloomberg and Politico reported.
  • This means that overall tariffs wouldn’t exceed 15% for the EU, Japan, and South Korea, for example, while China’s rate could climb to 20%—likely higher than many other nations.

All this comes as the White House looks to replace President Trump’s initial batch of tariffs that the Supreme Court invalidated in February. He was expected to try again under different laws, including…

…Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act, which allows for tariffs that address unfair economic practices. US officials have accused other countries, especially China, of harming American manufacturers by churning out an oversupply of cheap products. The US launched a Section 301 investigation into this alleged excess manufacturing capacity in March. It’s expected to release its findings and proposed new tariffs as soon as this week, though that timing could reportedly change.

Party pooper?

A fresh round of levies could make all those handshakes between world leaders especially aggressive and/or awkward at next month’s G20 meeting in Miami. For that reason, some trade experts told Bloomberg that they think the US will wait on the new tariffs until after the summit (and until the US Court of International Trade decides on forced-labor tariffs that Trump unveiled in July).

Meanwhile…the levies could also further frustrate Americans who swung blue in the midterm elections due to cost-of-living concerns.—ML

items.summary: A historian gave GPT-6.2 Astra a mystery he had investigated for years. Within 22 minutes, the AI identified a likely artist and located an archival reference that led to the discovery of a 162-page historical journal.
items.author: Marianne Sison
items.contentHtml:

GPT-6.2 Astra Helped Solve a 200-Year-Old Historical Mystery in 22 Minutes

A historian gave GPT-6.2 Astra a mystery he had investigated for years. Within 22 minutes, the AI identified a likely artist and located an archival reference that led to the discovery of a 162-page historical journal.

Written By
Marianne Sison
Nov 25, 2026
· 3 minute read

Back in 2022, historian Mark Humphries came across an old sketchbook at Yale University. It contained drawings from a trip through Canada and the Great Lakes in 1808, but nobody knew who drew them.

Humphries had spent hours trying to figure it out over the years. So when he got early access to OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra, he decided to give the AI a shot at solving the mystery.

As Humphries explained in a November 24 blog post, Astra came back with a name in just 22 minutes and one second. Even better, it found a reference to a 162-page travel journal that would help him confirm the artist's identity.

How Astra cracked the case

The 84-page sketchbook contained illustrations of historical sites, some of which no longer exist. Humphries had a few guesses about who the artist might be, and he shared those with Astra along with some historical context.

Astra quickly ruled out his original suspects because their whereabouts didn't match the dates on the drawings. Instead, it came up with someone Humphries had never heard of: Louis-Guy-Charles-Guillaume de Rohan-Chabot, a French aristocrat who served in the British Army.

Advertisement

So how did Astra land on this guy?

One of the clues came from the diary of Joseph Frobisher, a retired fur trader who kept records of his social engagements in Montreal. According to his diary, Chabot left Lachine on June 6, 1808. Other historical correspondence placed him at Fort St. Joseph later that month.

The dates matched, but Humphries still needed evidence that Chabot was the person behind the drawings.

Here's where things get interesting. Astra had dug up a footnote in a 2014 doctoral thesis about French refugees. The footnote referenced Chabot's travel journal, a microfilmed copy of which was available at Cleveland State University.

Humphries got hold of the journal and compared it with the sketchbook. The handwriting and travel dates matched. Then he came across a particularly revealing entry from June 18, 1808, in which Chabot described his visit to Fort St. Joseph and wrote, “I took a sketch.”

His description matched one of the drawings in Yale's collection.

Advertisement

And just like that, Humphries had evidence of who drew the pictures, plus an entire travel journal that could teach historians more about the North American fur trade.

What else could AI help historians discover?

Think about how much historical information is tucked away in old diaries, academic footnotes, and archival collections. Unless researchers know what they're looking for, they may never come across some of these documents.

What's exciting about this experiment is how Astra figured out which records were worth investigating. It followed clues across different sources and found a document that could help answer the original question.

Humphries also tried the experiment with Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2. It came up with the same name in about 35 minutes, although it missed the travel journal.

Interestingly, even after Humphries presented Astra with the additional evidence, the model still had doubts because the journal lacked a signature. The historian had to assess the evidence himself and decide how much confidence to place in the discovery.

We've seen AI help solve mathematical problems and decipher encrypted historical messages. Now we're getting a better sense of how these models could contribute to historical research.

Advertisement

For researchers with limited time and funding, an AI agent could make it possible to investigate questions they've had on the back burner for years. Who knows how many other historical mysteries could be solved with documents already sitting in university archives?

Everything That Happened in AI Today (Wednesday, November 25, 2026)

OpenAI demonstrated GPT-6's protein-design capabilities; Astra helped amateur astronomers identify potential exoplanets; Anthropic expanded Claude's agent capabilities; Midjourney released Niji V8; and PrismML introduced a compact coding model.

Written By
Marianne Sison
Nov 25, 2026
· 6 minute read

GPT-6 is venturing into biology, where proteins designed by the AI showed evidence of binding to five targets in laboratory experiments.

Welcome, humans!

Today's AI news takes us from the biology lab to outer space. Two amateur astronomers used AI to search NASA telescope data for undiscovered planets, while another experiment explored whether Astra could solve an open historical mystery. There's even a new mathematical preprint from OpenAI.

Meanwhile, Claude can now turn artifacts into desktop apps, Meta is bringing Muse into Instagram DMs, and a 27-billion-parameter model promises better coding capabilities with just 5.9 GB of storage. Apparently, our computers have quite a few career options now.

Let's get into it.

🆕 NEW From The Neuron

  • What Happens After AGI? Google DeepMind researchers explored four possible routes to superintelligence, including a future where millions of AI agents work together.
  • Can AI Spot Breast Cancer Earlier? The NHS is testing AI-assisted breast cancer screening with nearly 700,000 women to determine whether AI can improve detection rates and reduce radiologists' workloads.
Advertisement

Around the Horn: Wednesday, November 25, 2026

GPT-6 is learning to design proteins

OpenAI demonstrated GPT-6's protein-design capabilities, showing that its general-purpose AI models can use reasoning and code to design protein sequences and predict their physical forms. Laboratory experiments subsequently found evidence of binding across five targets.

Proteins consist of chains of amino acids that fold into three-dimensional shapes. Those shapes influence how proteins interact with other molecules in the body. Designing proteins that bind to specific targets could eventually help researchers develop new medicines or investigate biological processes.

The results suggest that general-purpose reasoning models could contribute to work typically associated with specialized biological AI systems. There's still a considerable distance between demonstrating protein binding and developing a safe, effective treatment. The next question is whether GPT-6 can produce reliable designs across a wider range of biological targets.

Advertisement

🏆 TOP 5 NEWS (Around the Horn)

  • OpenAI's Astra helped amateur astronomers identify potential exoplanets using Codex and publicly available observations from NASA's Kepler and TESS space telescopes.
  • OpenAI published a mathematical preprint that claims a matrix multiplication exponent of 9/4, a result that could have implications for the computational efficiency of multiplying matrices if independently validated.
  • GPT-6.2 Astra reportedly investigated an unresolved historical mystery through autonomous research, hypothesis formation, and evidence analysis.
  • OpenClaw research questioned AI agent reliability as businesses increasingly adopt autonomous systems. As The Neuron's coverage of ShellBench explains, changing the software that manages an AI model's execution can affect its performance by nearly 10 percentage points.
  • Over two dozen sources told Axios that employees at OpenAI and Anthropic are concerned about whether some advanced AI models can be released safely as their capabilities increase.
Advertisement

Honorable Mentions

  • Novartis CEO Vas Narasimhan predicted that AI could cut four years from drug development timelines, while questioning predictions that AI will cure diseases such as cancer within a decade.
  • Anthropic researchers revisited neuron-level interpretability, addressing three objections to studying individual artificial neurons. A companion research article explored how this approach could contribute to AI safety.
  • White Circle announced a post-training competition alongside organizations including OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Mistral AI, with $1.5 million in computing resources and over $200,000 in cash prizes for participants who improve AI models after their initial training.
  • The US blacklisted Megaspeed, the company connected to the controversy surrounding Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia. Huang still faces congressional scrutiny over chip export controls, while his return has drawn attention to US-China competition for AI talent.
Advertisement

🍪 TOP TREATS TO TRY

  • Anthropic made Claude artifacts installable as desktop apps on Mac and Windows, complete with connected services, optional notifications, and menu bar integration.
  • Anthropic announced Skills over MCP and Tasks on the second anniversary of the Model Context Protocol, the standard for connecting AI applications to external tools and data. The protocol is expanding toward communication and coordination between AI agents.
  • Phylo introduced Biomni Swarm, a team of AI agents designed to collaborate on complex biomedical research questions.
  • PrismML released Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B, a compact AI model that improves coding, repeated tool interactions, and multistep task execution within a 5.9 GB footprint.
  • Midjourney launched Niji V8, its latest anime image-generation model, with improved prompt accuracy, character consistency, visual coherence, and a dedicated editing model.
  • Meta integrated Muse into Instagram DMs, so users can interact with its AI agent directly from their messages. Meta also partnered with Walmart to make Black Friday deals accessible through Muse.
  • The UAE introduced an AI education assistant that analyzes existing school records to identify areas where children may need additional academic support.
  • Instantly launched PULSE-1, a proprietary AI sales model trained on billions of go-to-market data points that the company claims can generate up to 2.2 times more positive replies. Users can try it for free until December 1.
  • Pinterest introduced parental controls that allow parents to limit how much AI-generated content appears in their teenagers' feeds.
  • Granular.Build introduced a visual workspace where a coordinating AI agent delegates tasks to specialized agents, manages project files, and helps users create apps or multimedia projects with live previews.
  • Clam AI introduced permission-based email access for AI agents, allowing Gmail users to define in plain language which messages agents can access and which actions they can perform.
Advertisement

🏢 Big Tech & Major Companies

  • Anthropic shares plunged on Tuesday as investor concerns about the AI market resurfaced after the initial optimism over Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia.
  • Tidal announced plans to remove millions of fully AI-generated music tracks from its streaming service. The platform will continue to accept AI-assisted music.

🤖 AI Agents & Infrastructure

  • Epochal introduced its research vision for AI systems that learn from past events and experience, with accurate predictions of future outcomes as a measure of intelligence.
  • A Crusoe investor advocated for solar power and battery storage as energy sources for future AI data centers, which could require tens of gigawatts of power.
Advertisement

🏛️ AI Policy, Governance & Safety

  • The UK's Financial Conduct Authority outlined its regulatory expectations for financial services firms, technology providers, and social media platforms that develop or deploy autonomous AI products.
  • Amazon detected an open-source AI agent that reportedly exploited a previously unknown software vulnerability to gain unauthorized access with limited human intervention.
  • Anthropic developed a honeypot test that presents AI agents with opportunities to misbehave and evaluates whether they resist those temptations.
  • A former OpenAI employee was granted release on a $1 million bond following allegations that he planted a surveillance device in a company conference room. The judge found insufficient grounds to justify continued detention before trial.
Advertisement

📊 Fundraising & Deals Roundup

  • Maple raised $5.3 million to develop encrypted AI products designed to prevent unauthorized access to users' private data, including access by Maple itself.

💡 Industry Commentary & Analysis

  • OpenAI researcher Noam Brown urged promising students to consider leaving school to participate in AI development. The o1 co-creator acknowledged current limitations in planning and self-correction but expects AI progress to accelerate as models contribute to the development of their successors.

Previous Around the Horn Digests

Catch up on everything you missed:

  • Tuesday, November 24, 2026: Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia, DeepMind improved quantum algorithms, and the NHS launched an AI cancer-screening trial.
  • Monday, November 23, 2026: AI agents designed a CPU, Claude contributed to a mathematical proof, and OpenAI proposed a shared AI progress metric.
  • Friday, November 20, 2026: Anthropic made its stock market debut, Meta faced Muse privacy concerns, and Gemini gained computer-use capabilities on Mac.
  • Thursday, November 19, 2026: Anthropic priced its $81.3 billion IPO, Nvidia halted AI chip shipments to China, and Google unveiled Gemini 4 Neon.
  • Wednesday, November 18, 2026: OpenAI launched GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, Google revised Gemini's privacy controls, and Microsoft introduced cheaper coding models.
  • Tuesday, November 17, 2026: California sued OpenAI, the US tightened AI chip export controls, and Apple tested daily limits for Siri AI.
  • Monday, November 16, 2026: OpenAI introduced ChatGPT Wallet, Jensen Huang considered returning to Nvidia, and Disney expanded its AI ambitions.

That's a Wrap
