items.title: Why neutrality is worth chasing, even if no one gets there
items.summary: Critics say neutrality is impossible, but Jimmy Wales, founder of Wikipedia and author of The Seven Rules of Trust , argues that this is no reason to stop trying. In this conversation with Jonny Thomson, he explains why a fight over a single word, from “Gdańsk” to “security…
items.author: Jonny Thomson, Jimmy Wales
items.contentHtml:
Critics say neutrality is impossible, but Jimmy Wales, founder of Wikipedia and author of The Seven Rules of Trust, argues that this is no reason to stop trying. In this conversation with Jonny Thomson, he explains why a fight over a single word, from “Gdańsk” to “security fence,” is often what an encyclopedia should explain. He also says no one can fully see the biases built into AI models, and that people were cruel to each other online long before algorithms. The two also discuss why Wales won’t put money into Wikipedia editing and where editorial judgment ends and censorship begins. They close with his optimistic view of the next 20 years.

This video Why neutrality is worth chasing, even if no one gets there is featured on Big Think.

items.title: Ease productivity overload with “niksen,” the Dutch art of doing nothing
items.summary: When was the last time you did nothing? By that, I don’t mean scrolling through social media, mowing the lawn, or fretting over the latest office drama. I mean a do-nothingness with no purpose and no goal other than to just enjoy being. If you’re like most modern adults, you’ll…
items.author: Kevin Dickinson
items.contentHtml:
When was the last time you did nothing? By that, I don’t mean scrolling through social media, mowing the lawn, or fretting over the latest office drama. I mean a do-nothingness with no purpose and no goal other than to just enjoy being. 

If you’re like most modern adults, you’ll likely have trouble recalling such a luxurious moment, and even if you could, would you openly admit it? The more you think about it, the more you realize how incredibly difficult it is not only to find the time for nothing but to own it without embarrassment.

In our work- and improvement-focused culture, doing nothing isn’t the mark of time well-spent. Check the dictionary, and you won’t find a positive-sounding label for a do-nothing. You will, however, discover a buffet of labels that discourage the very idea, with all the disappointment of a finger-wagging grandpa: deadbeat, laggard, lazybones, loafer, slacker, couch potato, and lotus eater. Little wonder then that we fill our schedules with work, activities, and chores under the pressure to constantly produce — even if such busywork is for the sake of performance.

But English may finally have a word that captures not only the joys of unoccupied moments but also the benefits they can bring. It’s niksen, and it’s on loan from the Netherlands.

Rebranding niksen

In its native Dutch, niksen means literally “to do nothing.” According to Maartje Williems, author of The Lost Art of Doing Nothing, the verb comes from the noun niks (nothing), and it wasn’t coined to be a ringing endorsement. This is evidenced by its lexical cousin niksnut — essentially, a layabout who does nothing and doesn’t contribute to society. (The Netherlands has its share of finger-wagging grandpas, too.)

But in the last decade, niksen has undergone a rebranding. In 2017, journalist Gebke Verhoeven published an article titled “Niksen Is the New Mindfulness” in the magazine Gezond Nu (Healthy Now). The article applied the Dutch verb to the benefits of relaxation that psychologists and sociologists were seeing in their research.

As Verhoeven wrote: “We cram our free time so that we don’t have a minute left to just do nothing. Is that bad? Yes, that’s bad. You don’t give your brain space and time to process information and feel what you really need. In short, you lose yourself a bit. High time to elevate idleness to art.”

The article inspired other journalists to explore the research under the label of niksen too — among them Olga Mecking, who wrote a popular piece on the subject for The New York Times. As if by providence, many of these articles came out in 2019, just before the COVID-19 pandemic abruptly forced people to reconsider how they spend their idle time.

For the record, Dutch isn’t the first language to coin a term for the splendor of laziness. Italian, for example, has the tasty expression la dolce far niente (literally, “sweet doing nothing”). It doesn’t get as much play today, as it sounds a bit dated and cliched to modern ears. The expression did, however, serve as the inspiration for several works of art, including a series of oil paintings by Neoclassicist John William Godward.

But it seems niksen — admittedly more compact — has gained widespread acceptance as the word to represent the concept today.

How does one practice niksen?

To niksen, you only need to be idle for a time without trying to be productive or fulfill a purpose. That’s it. It sounds as easy as curling up in your favorite chair. Yet in practice, it’s far more difficult.

Imagine you work remotely, and you take a break to clean out the dishwasher. Is that niksen? No. You’re using your time to be productive, and that’s not doing nothing. What about scrolling through your Instagram feed instead? Again, no. You’ve used the time to catch up with all the online happenings.

Even if you sit doing nothing, your mind can betray your endeavors. Spending the time planning out an upcoming presentation means you’re still at work. And despite the title of Verhoeven’s 2017 article, mindfulness isn’t niksen either. Mindfulness has the explicit goal of being fully present in the moment. Meanwhile, niksen’s purpose-free musings are more akin to mindlessness.

So what does count? Staring out the window and watching birds flit around. Enjoying the aroma of your coffee as it brews in the morning. Having a pleasant daydream as music plays in the background. Sitting in a cafe and watching the people pass by. It’s any “unguarded moment,” Williems writes, of “having nothing to do and not finding something new to do.”

Beyond that, there are no hard-and-fast rules. Williems recommends the moments be spontaneous, have no time limit, and be in a distraction-free environment. But Carolien Hamming, managing director of CSR Centrum, a stress coaching center, advises you to schedule sessions and use a timer, especially if you’re just starting out. Some even suggest incorporating an easygoing activity with no specific goal. Think walking, knitting, pen spinning, or brewing a cup of tea. 

“Dare to be idle,” Hamming told TIME. “It is all about allowing life to run its course, and to free us from obligations for just a moment.”

The benefits of being a do-nothing

I am unaware of any studies that have specifically looked at niksen as detailed above. The concept is likely too new and amorphous. We’ll have to wait and see. That said, much research points to the benefits of rest and relaxation, and niksen could offer similar benefits for people who find the practice checks both boxes.

One such benefit is improved focus and decision-making. Your frontal lobe — a section of the brain involved in decision-making and self-control — grows fatigued the more cognitive load is put on it. When you rest, your frontal lobe throttles down and lets your default mode network take over. This different brain state reduces the cognitive load, so your frontal lobe has more energy when you return to your daily to-dos. 

While your brain revives most during sleep, research shows that resting throughout the day can boost your mental performance. As Emily Maloney wrote about her niksen experience for The Washington Post: “These breaks in my day were most helpful when I was tired and needed a reset, when I was looking for space to be creative, or when I was having trouble focusing on a task I needed to do. Instead of fighting my natural rhythms, I gave in to them.”

Cognitive load can also explain why breaks that include chores, social media scrolling, and the like aren’t as effective. Rather than letting your frontal lobe wind down, they thrust a whole new set of decisions and self-control challenges at it.

Meaningful breaks have been shown to help reduce stress, too. While some stress can motivate you to accomplish a task or rise to a challenge, too much stress or stress held for too long can harm your performance and productivity. It isn’t great for your health and well-being either. By building relaxing moments into your days, you can better balance your stress levels by tapping into your “rest-and-digest” response (the counterpart to the more famous “fight-or-flight” response). These breaks can also help you create better boundaries between times of rest and those of intense focus.

“Niksen appeals to a desire for a simpler, more minimal lifestyle,” Mecking writes in her book, Niksen: Embracing the Dutch Art of Doing Nothing. “As you become comfortable with niksen, you will also become more comfortable with refusing to be so busy. Niksen will help you let go of some of that busyness instead of adding to it.”

Finally, creativity and problem-solving can also be boosted by moments of respite. According to Emma Seppälä, associate director of the Center for Compassion and Altruism Research and Education, research shows creative thinking is at its peak when our brains are swimming in slow-moving alpha and delta brain waves. These waves are most prominent when you are at rest, and your default mode network is activated.

“So if you remain focused all the time — constantly doing, doing, doing — you’re not allowing yourself into that mode that will actually lead to the greatest creativity that you have,” Seppälä said in an interview with Big Think.

Balancing niksen with something

I’ve previously written about how a wandering mind can lead to unhappiness, boredom can be a warning, and daydreaming can cause distress. That may suggest that shying away from doing nothing is wise in most respects. But it’s worth reiterating that these normal mental happenings only become problematic when they interrupt the moments during which we want to pay attention: work projects we find meaningful, evenings out with family, and hobbies that bring joy to our lives.

It’s about balance. We need moments to breathe and recover, so when we return to the active part of our lives, we’re fully engaged and appreciative. At the same time, our active lives should allow us to appreciate the joys of just being without a sense of guilt.

As Rutt Veenhoven, a sociologist at Erasmus University Rotterdam, told Vogue: “The pace of life today is fast because there is much to enjoy. This is one of the reasons for the high level of happiness in modern society. Activity is a powerful driver of happiness, both because it keeps us fit and because active people build up more resources in work and relationships.”

He added: “Niksen provides a relief for people who feel overwhelmed by the pace. It is also an attractive idea for those who are not overwhelmed but still feel the pressure, too.”

Does niksen work? For some people, yes. For others, maybe not. It depends on how we, as individuals, find relief from the constant hustle of modern life. But make no mistake: We all need that relief.

This article Ease productivity overload with “niksen,” the Dutch art of doing nothing is featured on Big Think.

items.title: The Cyclical Nature of Love
items.summary: Welcome to The Unsolicited Advice Reading Group. This month we are reading Anne Carson’s book Eros The Bittersweet . Our schedule will be as follows: Saturday 7th November - Up to “Alphabetic Edge” Saturday 14th November - Up to “Folded Meanings” Saturday 21st November - Up to…
items.author: Joseph Folley
items.contentHtml:
Welcome to The Unsolicited Advice Reading Group. This month we are reading Anne Carson’s book Eros The Bittersweet. Our schedule will be as follows:

Saturday 7th November - Up to “Alphabetic Edge”

Saturday 14th November - Up to “Folded Meanings”

Saturday 21st November - Up to “Cicadas” (sorry, travelling is still pretty intense)

Saturday 28th November - Up to the end

Saturday 5th December - Live call for paid subscribers (6PM UK time)

If you would like to read exclusive articles and join our live calls, consider becoming a paid subscriber :)

Carson’s book is structured such that it often sits somewhere between an aphoristic work and a collection of mini-essays, loosely but not totally related to one another. As we talked about last week, the book contains a kind of yearning structure, where it comes back to the same topics, each time making slightly more progress in its analysis, and then revisiting the same territory, and sometimes even repeating the same points, a few pages later. This means that any kind of writing on her book will always leave many of her points on the table, as the more fragmentary observations get skimmed over in favour of her more detailed points. So today I want to simply talk about the way Carson plays with time in two chapters: the one titled “Ice-pleasure” and the one titled “Now Then”. Specifically, let’s look at this observation, which Carson makes about an except of Sophocles’ poetry which likens desire to the pleasure of holding ice in your hands, which at first can be quite nice, but then your hand is too cold to hold the ice comfortably, and you can’t put it down because it has begun to melt. Thus, the lover is pulled “to act and not to act, again and again”. This is what Carson has to say about the image:

“The desire at the end of the poem is desire as repetition - exerting its pull “over and over again”. So time forms a ring around desire. Now, as you peer down through concentric circles of time, you see at the heart of the poem a piece of ice, melting. The startling likeness of ice drops into your perception with a shock like what the children must feel in their hands. The poem places you for shock, at an interface between two kinds of time, each of which spirals with its own logic upward through the structure of the poem, and through the psychology of desire.”

The two kinds of time that Carson references are the novelty of holding ice in your hands, and the inevitable end to this novelty which is brought on either by the melting of the ice or the simple passage of time. The image of the ice is compelling, but I think we might just as well think of the way that a young child will request a toy, throw it away, and then request it again. We find this funny as adults, but it is not clear that our desires are any different. They also, for Carson, contain this paradoxical structure. The tension is contained within the fact that the pleasurable sensation is in the ice melting, but that melting is the very thing that makes the experience ephemeral and unable-to-be-fixed. Hence why Carson describes desire as in the structure of a circle.

Of course, Carson is not the first person to make this observation (indeed, to hear her tell it, Sophocles already knew this, and he was drawing on an already established image that his audience would recognise). The image of the circle to illustrate something about desire is found in the book of Ecclesiastes, which famously couches its images of despair in terms of cycles. Within the first few lines we get this:

“The sun rises and the sun sets,

and hurries back to where it rises.

The wind blows to the south

and turns to the north;

round and round it goes,

ever returning on its course.”

This is, of course, a pessimistic spin on things. In Schopenhauer we get a similar kind of desire-structure. Perhaps Schopenhauer’s most famous line is “life swings back and forth like a pendulum between frustration and boredom”, but we might as easily substitute in a circle. Both because a pendulum kind of is already a circle, or at the very least cyclical, but also because because Schopenhauer’s pessimistic theory of desire is, if anything, more like a circle than a pendulum. We must remember that for Schopenhauer boredom just is a will to have some kind of desire to pursue, and that boredom sets in when all determinate desires are sated. Thus, we can picture Schopenhauer’s alternation between boredom and frustration as the continual cycle of having an unsated desire (and thus being in frustration), achieving that desire, desiring desire itself (that is, being bored), and then getting a new desire and re-entering frustration. It is a much more extreme kind of hedonic treadmill than the one we might find in Epicurus or Seneca.

Thus, by presenting the structure of desire as cyclical, we might expect that Carson, much like in the Sophocles excerpt, would consider eros as a kind of disease. This might seem even more likely when we consider her further claim that eros is something inflicted on the participant from the outside (again, much like Schopenhauer’s desires, which for the unascetic person emerge almost of their own accord). All of this points towards a kind of pessimism about eros. I personally think that a pessimistic interpretation of Carson’s observations would be totally coherent, but it is not the path that Carson decides the take, and her book is more interesting for its refusal to embrace an ascetic answer to the problem of eros, and, like so many great wise men throughout history, recommend that we try to become unmoved by it. Carson has no knockdown explicit argument for this optimism in the way an analytic philosopher would recognise, it emerges from a series of broader observations she makes. If I were to try to reconstruct her argument, it would probably be a kind of reductio argument. Eros is such a powerful and fulfilling experience that any philosophy that exiles it from the “Good Life” must be discarded, but to embrace eros we must also find some way of appreciating this cyclical structure of desire.

In this way Carson’s book becomes strangely Nietzschean. In Bernard Reginster’s interpretation of the Eternal Recurrence (which remains one of my favourites) he links it to the Will to Power, which he interprets as the “will to overcome resistance”. That is, he thinks the Will to Power is the second-order desire to overcome some definite resistance to a first-order desire. We might notice that this is actually quite similar to Schopenhauer’s structure of the will, but with a more optimistic interpretation (Reginster in fact begins his analysis of the Will to Power by stating he wants to take seriously Nietzsche’s claim that it is a substitute for the Schopenhauerian Will to Live). However, if what is really desired is to overcome resistance to a determinate first-order desire, then the frustration of an unfulfilled desire is not necessarily a negative thing, but instead is a necessary part of what a person (or a drive, if you want to take this interpretation subpersonally) “really wants”. Thus, when Nietzsche says in Ecce Homo that the eternal recurrence is the highest form of affirmation, we must remember that the eternal recurrence is a world where there simply is no such thing as a closed desire. All resistances will come around again and have to be overcome afresh. Thus, someone who could affirm the eternal recurrence is someone with a strong will to power (at least, if we take Reginster’s interpretation). With this in mind, Carson’s admiration for eros despite its circular nature is not too dissimilar from the kind of affirmation found here in Nietzsche. To embrace Eros as Carson defines it must be to embrace this circular structure of desire, and inasmuch as this is the case, it pushes through the pessimism of Schopenhauer to the task of affirming impermanence, though in a different way to Reginster’s Nietzsche. Eros necessarily involves an ebb and flow, and so is antithetical to the idea of a permanent rest or a Heavenly beatitude. It is no wonder that Jesus said that no one in Heaven would marry, but they would instead “live like angels” - that is, they would live in an eternal way, rather than a temporal way. Such a state precludes Eros.

Of course, this cyclical structure also has straightforward implications for how we think about interpersonal love. I mentioned before that Esther Perel talks about the importance of a sense of separation in relationships, as well as of melding. If we incorporate the circle into this, then we find that Eros, were it to last over a long period of time, would probably involve an alternation between distance and closeness, whereby the lover is reminded of the distance between them and their beloved, overcomes that distance, only to have some new distance reinstated. I think there is something in this, but at the same time I wonder how to separate this kind of desirable Eros-creation from an undesirable “hot and cold” dynamic. A hot and cold dynamic is notorious for causing both intense suffering and intense desire, and most people I’ve spoken to find it highly eros-laden but ultimately unsustainable. Is there a version of Eros which keeps a desirable kind of distance-closeness cycle, without giving into outright unsustainable unpleasantness? I am not totally sure. I have some sketch ideas, like the teasing I mentioned in a previous post, but nothing concrete. Though perhaps that is only appropriate, given what Carson says elsewhere about the incompleteness of any analysis of love.

I like this idea of cycles in Eros because I think it represents temporally the bittersweetness that Carson has been continually referencing. In her initial observations about Sappho’s poetry, Carson largely wrote about the simultaneous existence of joy and suffering that occurred with a yearnful love. But this is not the only way that bittersweetness appears. It can also involve an alternation between certain bitter elements and certain sweet elements. The moment of feeling closer to your beloved is a triumph, and the moment their separateness becomes apparent is bitter, but that bitterness is necessary in order that further sweetness may ensue. There is glukupikron both horizontally and vertically.

items.title: OpenClaw’s ShellBench Is an AI Benchmark I’d Actually Use
items.summary: The same AI model can gain or lose nearly 10 percentage points when you swap the software around it. OpenClaw’s ShellBench puts those differences to the test on the messy, ordinary work people actually hand to agents.
items.author: Corey Noles
items.contentHtml:
SHARE
Add The Neuron as a preferred source

OpenClaw’s ShellBench Is an AI Benchmark I’d Actually Use

The same AI model can gain or lose nearly 10 percentage points when you swap the software around it. OpenClaw’s ShellBench puts those differences to the test on the messy, ordinary work people actually hand to agents.

Written By
Corey Noles
Nov 24, 2026
· 3 minute read

Run OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra through Pi and it passes 65.3% of the tasks in OpenClaw’s new ShellBench benchmark. Run the same model through Claude Code and it passes 55.4%. Claude Fable 5.2 goes the other way, scoring 61.0% in Pi and 63.0% in Claude Code. Change the software around the models and the two trade places on the leaderboard.

I’m usually skeptical of AI benchmarks. A leaderboard can tell me which model edged out another by a point. I rarely know what I’m supposed to do with that information on Monday morning. ShellBench gives me a way to see whether the agent setup I’m considering is worth trying on my own work, or whether I'm doing my best to set myself up for success.

The OpenClaw Foundation and collaborators including Parsewave, Hugging Face, Red Hat, and UC Berkeley built ShellBench around 100 tasks informed by patterns in more than 10 million anonymized agent interactions. The release covers 12 models, five harnesses, and 53,100 graded runs. On the 90 tasks scored with a rubric, the median prompt was 43 words and the median workspace held 188 files. If you’ve ever written “Can you figure out which version is current?” and pointed someone at a shared drive, you get the idea. The full research paper was still forthcoming at the time of the announcement.

The harness is part of what you’re buying

Advertisement

An AI harness is the software that gives a model its tools, manages what it sees, and determines how it can act. Claude Code, Codex CLI, Hermes, OpenClaw, and Pi all fill that role. The same model can work differently depending on how the harness handles files, tool errors, and what stays in context.

Model choice made the bigger difference across the full field. Within a harness, the median spread between the best and worst models was 45.7 percentage points. Keeping the model fixed and switching harnesses produced a median spread of 6.2 points. Among the five highest-scoring models, those spreads were 15.2 and 9.9 points, respectively. That’s the comparison I’d care about if I already had a shortlist of strong models.

Speed can break an apparent tie, too. Across the 11 models tested in all five harnesses, OpenClaw and Pi averaged virtually identical pass rates. Pi’s median run took 1.31 minutes, compared with 2.86 for OpenClaw. And on the model side, GPT-6.1 Sol came within 1.1 percentage points of Astra’s overall pass rate at roughly one-sixth the estimated token cost per run. Those are differences a team can feel once an agent starts doing the same job hundreds of times.

Advertisement

The benchmark gets interesting when the agent fails

In one dinner-planning task, agents picked the right restaurant in 522 of 531 attempts. Only 152 attempts met every requirement. In 331 runs, the sole miss was failing to name the files that backed up the budget or timing. For dinner, you might shrug and book the table. When someone asks why the agent used one invoice over another, those missing receipts are suddenly the whole conversation.

Repeatability matters just as much. Across the five harnesses, GPT-6 Astra passed 75.1% of tasks at least once in three tries and 48.8% on all three. OpenClaw says some of that variation could come from grading, since each run was judged once. The study also found that 9.9% of runs that cleared every correctness check still missed a safety requirement. A polished answer tells you very little about what happened along the way.

Here’s what I’d borrow from ShellBench. Take a recurring task your team already does, give two agent setups the same messy inputs, and run each a few times. Check what a human has to verify or redo before the result can go out the door. That review time belongs in the cost of the agent, right alongside the tokens. The vendors that make the work easier to check have something real to compete on, even when their model sits a point down the leaderboard.

Advertisement

  • DeepSeek’s own tests show how much a coding score can move while the underlying model stays fixed. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Explained
  • Meta-Harness explores whether an agent can improve the instructions, tools, and workflow around a model automatically. Meta-Harness Makes the Case for Automated AI Agents

Corey Noles

items.title: 3 keys will unlock the next level in how the Universe began
items.summary: In all the Universe, there’s no bigger question — and no greater mystery — than where all of this came from, and how all of this came to be. For countless generations, our cosmic origins were a question for poets, theologians, and philosophers, as our scientific knowledge had…
items.author: Ethan Siegel
items.contentHtml:
In all the Universe, there’s no bigger question — and no greater mystery — than where all of this came from, and how all of this came to be. For countless generations, our cosmic origins were a question for poets, theologians, and philosophers, as our scientific knowledge had not yet advanced to the point where we could uncover an evidence-based answer to such questions. However, the 20th and 21st centuries changed all of that, allowing us to pin down the answers to such questions as:

  • What rules govern our Universe?
  • What is the Universe made of?
  • How large and how old is it?
  • How did it come to be the way it is today?
  • And what are our ultimate cosmic origins?

We often say, now, that our Universe began with the hot Big Bang, but that’s only the Universe as we know and experience it today: the observable Universe. We’ve since learned that the Big Bang itself was preceded and set up by an earlier phase in cosmic history: cosmic inflation, where space itself contained an enormous amount of inherent energy and expanded — or inflated — rapidly and relentlessly. When inflation ended, our hot Big Bang ensued, giving rise to the Universe as we know, observe, and exist within it.

But what, exactly, were inflation’s properties? What type of inflation occurred, and what relics, or imprints, of inflation remain within our observable Universe today? Although we’ve come remarkably far in our understanding of our cosmic origins, there are a few windows still left unexplored that can take our understanding to the next level. Here are the three big ones where new data will help guide the way.

We truly went from not knowing what the Universe was, at all, to figuring out an enormous amount about our cosmic origins in the span of less than 150 years. Our journey began in earnest in the late 19th century, when people began to notice breakdowns in Newtonian mechanics at speeds close to the speed of light, and hints of a breakdown in Newtonian gravity when it came to the orbit of the planet Mercury. Both of those puzzles were eventually resolved with Einstein and relativity: special relativity for Newtonian mechanics, and general relativity, incorporating gravity in a relativistic framework, to eventually resolve the precession of Mercury’s perihelion.

Within that new framework for gravity, several new exact solutions emerged. These included the:

  • Minkowski solution, which reduces to flat, uncurved, matter-free space,
  • Schwarzschild solution, for a non-rotating black hole,
  • de Sitter solution, for a Universe dominated by a cosmological constant, and
  • Friedmann solution, for a Universe that was both isotropic (the same in all directions) and homogeneous (the same in all locations) and filled evenly with at least one form of energy.

Friedmann’s solution, derived in 1922, was particularly interesting from a cosmic perspective, because it showed that static spacetimes that were uniformly filled with “stuff” were unstable; the Universe must expand or contract.

Contemporaneously, starting in 1923, we began identifying individual stars within the spiral and elliptical nebulae in the skies: determining that they were galaxies beyond the Milky Way. When we combined those distance measurements with redshift measurements, or how fast these galaxies appeared to recede from us, we found a relationship: the farther the galaxy, the faster the recession speed. When this relationship was placed into the context of Friedmann’s solution, we arrived at the expanding Universe: the first big step toward understanding our cosmic origins.

If the Universe is expanding today, then that means things are getting farther apart, becoming less dense, and — since the wavelength of radiation is stretching to become longer — cooling as well. If things are getting less dense and cooling today, that means that they were denser and hotter in the past. Since gravitation attracts objects and brings them together, the Universe should become more structure rich, i.e., clumpier, as time goes on as well. Therefore, this points toward an early state of the Universe that was hotter, denser, and more uniform than it is today.

If you start off with a very hot, very dense, very uniform, and rapidly expanding Universe, then as time goes on, the following sets of things will occur.

  1. Particles will clump together, forming protons and neutrons, and then protons and neutrons will fuse together into atomic nuclei: creating an initial set of elements even before stars have formed.
  2. Atomic nuclei and electrons will combine together, and as the Universe cools sufficiently to make stable, neutral atoms, any photons (or radiation) that was present back then will simply stream outward in a straight line, stretching in wavelength and cooling as the Universe expands to create a persistent background of radiation: the CMB.
  3. Gravitation will pull matter together into clumps: creating stars, star clusters, small galaxies, larger galaxies, groups and clusters of galaxies, and even grander structures akin to a cosmic web. As time goes on, this web-like structure gets more well-defined and more pronounced.
  4. And the Universe keeps on expanding, with the expansion rate changing as the density of the Universe changes, resulting in a particular relationship between the expansion rate over time and the matter-and-energy contents of the Universe.

These are the four cornerstones of the hot Big Bang, and all four have been observationally confirmed.

However, at the same time, the Big Bang can’t be extrapolated all the way back to arbitrarily early times, high temperatures, and high densities. If we could, we’d see large differences in temperatures in different directions, which we don’t see. We’d see departures from cosmic flatness in different directions, which we don’t see. And we’d see leftover, high-energy relics from achieving super-high temperatures, which we don’t. Recognizing that we didn’t see these things served as the motivation for cosmic inflation, which posited a very different history for the early Universe.

Prior to being hot, dense, and filled with matter and radiation, the Universe was instead dominated by a large amount of inflationary — or field — energy that was inherent to space itself. This caused space to expand rapidly and relentlessly. This stretching of space gave it the same properties everywhere, made it indistinguishable from spatially flat, and inflated away any high-energy relics created in pre-inflationary times, solving all three of those cosmic puzzles.

In addition, several new predictions emerged from inflation that differed from the predictions of a non-inflationary hot Big Bang. They included:

  • A maximum early temperature well below the Planck temperature.
  • A spectrum of initial density fluctuations that was almost, but not quite perfectly, scale-invariant.
  • A set of cosmic density fluctuations that existed on scales larger than the cosmic horizon, seeded by inflationary processes.
  • And those fluctuations needed to be 100% adiabatic in nature, as opposed to isocurvature in nature.

In all of these cases, the data has come in, and favors inflation while disfavoring the Big Bang without inflation. Here in the 21st century, inflation has become the new standard for the origin of our cosmos.

However, there’s still a lot to learn about inflation. Open questions include:

  • What flavor of inflation occurred?
  • Which model for inflation is the most correct?
  • What was the (at least approximate) shape of the inflationary potential during that early period?
  • Were there gravitational wave fluctuations produced during inflation, and if so, what was their magnitude?
  • Does the spectral index, which describes the seed density fluctuations as a function of scale, run, or change in a complex fashion?
  • Are the density fluctuations perfectly Gaussian in nature — do they follow a bell curve — or are they non-Gaussianities?
  • And is that density fluctuation spectrum smooth all the way down to the smallest scales of all, or are there surprises, like big giant “spikes” in the distribution, on the tiniest scales of all?

These might seem like unanswerable questions, since by its very nature, inflation takes signals and stretches them to enormous, often unobservable scales. But those last few “doublings” of the cosmic horizon before the end of inflation do indeed leave imprints that remain in our Universe at the start of the hot Big Bang, and on a variety of scales: cosmic, large, intermediate, small, and very small scales.

In particular, this leads to three types of observational tests that we not only can perform to start to answer these questions, but tests that we’re actually on the cusp of performing in the very near future.

1.) Can we see evidence for primordial gravitational waves left over from inflation?

In addition to the spectrum of density fluctuations that arises from inflation, or scalar fluctuations, there should also be a spectrum of gravitational waves that comes from inflation as well, from tensor fluctuations. Whereas the density fluctuations provide the seeds of cosmic structure and lead to E-mode signals (or “circular” and “radial” features) that show up in the cosmic microwave background, the gravitational wave fluctuations provide a background “hum” on all cosmic scales and lead to B-mode signals (or swirling “clockwise” and “counterclockwise”) features in the CMB.

This can be searched for in a variety of ways. Gravitational wave experiments that are sensitive to low-frequency (large-scale) gravitational waves can detect or constrain such a background, dependent on its amplitude. The B-mode polarization pattern can be searched for through a variety of small-scale CMB experiments, again dependent on the (model-dependent) amplitude of the gravitational wave background. What inflation “fixes” is the spectrum of these B-mode (or gravitational wave) fluctuations, but the amplitude depends on which model, or flavor, of inflation actually applies to our Universe. Whether we measure the signal or simply set a limit on how large the signal can be, we learn more about our cosmic origins.

2.) Can we see evidence for particular models of inflation imprinted in the large-scale structure of the Universe?

Inflation produces an almost, but not quite, scale-invariant spectrum of density fluctuations in the Universe. On large cosmic scales, the magnitude of density fluctuations — i.e., how “overdense” or “underdense” each region is relative to the cosmic average — is slightly greater than it is on small scales, and this defines a quantity known as the spectra index, or the “tilt” of the spectrum. To a first approximation, these fluctuations are 100% Gaussian, or bell curve-like, in nature, and they fall off regularly, where the smaller the scale, the smaller the fluctuation, from large scales to small ones.

But there might be more to inflation than that simple first approximation. The density fluctuation spectrum doesn’t just tilt, it could also run. The fluctuations might not be perfectly Gaussian, but could display non-Gaussianity. Most models of inflation predict only a small amount, but with the right data, even a small amount could be detectable! We can probe this by creating large, deep, 3D surveys of the Universe to great precision and across cosmic time, and also by mapping out matter even where there’s no light: such as with 21-cm intensity mapping. These techniques will help us pin down the nature of inflation better than ever.

3.) Can the smallest cosmic scales reveal surprising features that only appear in certain models of or modifications to inflation?

And finally, on scales far, far smaller than large-scale structure endeavors can probe, inflation still creates those seed density fluctuations. Even though these scales are too small to be seen by CMB experiments, they persist in two places today:

  • in the substructures of dark matter halos, a relic of all the small clumps of matter and protogalaxies that fell into a larger-scale galaxy over time,
  • and in the high-redshift Universe, by probing the seed supermassive black holes that gave rise to the large, modern-day behemoths we find at the centers of the largest galaxies of all.

For the substructures in dark matter halos, we can probe these through a variety of techniques, such as the tracing out of the intracluster starlight by stripped stars in massive galaxy clusters, via large collections of quadruply lensed objects via strong gravitational lensing, or by the discovery of stellar streams and the tracing out of the gravitational potential that causes breaks and tails in them.

For seed supermassive black holes, we’ve already learned that overmassive black holes exist in the very young Universe: black holes that are just as massive or even more massive than all the stars in those host galaxies combined. Did these black holes arise from the collapse of cold gas hundreds of millions of years after the Big Bang? Or were they seeded long before that, by the process of cosmic inflation? Answering this question can either validate or invalidate standard inflationary models, and can do the same for exotic alternatives as well.

Even in modern-day textbooks and popular science textbooks, there are still those who question whether inflation actually happened or not: a viewpoint that’s now several decades out of date. Instead, the frontier has shifted just as it’s shifted with dark matter where active researchers no longer ask whether it’s real or not, but are working to determine what its specific properties are with observation-driven science. This requires an enormous suite of novel, cutting-edge facilities that can acquire superior data to help answer these questions.

  • For primordial gravitational waves, improved pulsar timing arrays, large-scale gravitational wave detectors, JAXA’s LiteBIRD mission, the Simons Observatory, and CMB S4 experiments can either find or place the greatest-ever constraints on their magnitude.
  • From large-scale structure, enormous surveys such as DESI, SPHEREx, Euclid, Roman, and Rubin can all map galaxies and starlight across cosmic time, while intensity mapping of the 21-cm neutral hydrogen signal, such as with CHIME or with the Square Kilometer Array (SKA), can map matter even where starlight is absent.
  • And to probe for small-scale structure, uncovering the origins of seed supermassive black holes, such as with JWST or even beyond its limits, as well as using stellar streams, the Lyman-α forest, and strong gravitational lenses to probe dark matter substructure within galaxies, can all test “regular” models of inflation against more exotic ones.

The acquisition of this data is the key to improving our understanding of how the Universe actually began. Here in the 21st century, asking for details about the “flavor” of inflation that occurred is the current frontier, and looking to the cosmic data itself will either enlighten us and tell us which type of inflation happened, place constraints on which types didn’t happen, or perhaps will even surprise us, and show us a Universe we never imagined was possible. Unless the day arrives where we cease to gather that necessary data and find out the answers, we guarantee that we’ll move forward in refining our understanding of how reality truly is.

This article 3 keys will unlock the next level in how the Universe began is featured on Big Think.

items.title: Grocery stores offer discounted Thanksgiving dinners at a loss
items.summary: Walmart It’s not just your silent cousin with a whole plate of mashed potatoes taking a huge hit for Thanksgiving dinner. Despite rising food prices, grocery chains like Walmart, Target, and Aldi are advertising heavily discounted holiday meal deals to woo customers—and maybe…
items.author: Matty Merritt
items.contentHtml:
It’s not just your silent cousin with a whole plate of mashed potatoes taking a huge hit for Thanksgiving dinner. Despite rising food prices, grocery chains like Walmart, Target, and Aldi are advertising heavily discounted holiday meal deals to woo customers—and maybe get them to spend money elsewhere in the store.

Grocery chains have been using holiday meal bundles for a while now to earn your loyalty, even if it means taking a loss. This year, Walmart’s deal, which the chain says can feed 10 people for $35, is one of the most affordable options out there.

  • The deal went viral when shoppers discovered they could pair it with a $10-off discount code, and workers at stores around the country reported a flood of orders.
  • Last week, CEO John Furner said in an earnings call that the retailer had already sold a million more turkeys in November than it did last year.

Zoom out: This year’s meal deals come as grocery prices remain stubbornly high, in part because the price of diesel has skyrocketed amid the war in Iran. The American Farm Bureau Federation said the average cost to feed 10 people for Thanksgiving increased 6% this year, the first time it’s gone up since 2022.—MM

items.title: Nvidia has a new CEO…Jensen Huang
items.summary: PHILIP FONG/Getty Images Nvidia went with an external candidate. In a spectacular about-face, the chipmaker reinstated Huang as its leader yesterday, 10 days after he was ousted for having multiple affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy allegedly involved in…
items.author: Sam Klebanov
items.contentHtml:
Nvidia went with an external candidate. In a spectacular about-face, the chipmaker reinstated Huang as its leader yesterday, 10 days after he was ousted for having multiple affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy allegedly involved in smuggling the company’s AI chips into China.

Nvidia said its board unanimously decided to bring Huang back and that his return doesn’t pose a national security risk, though outside counsel will keep investigating what happened. The company said the board had received input from senior levels of the US government.

How senior? President Trump told CNBC that he “spoke to” Nvidia’s board and “convinced them.” He also said he’d spoken to Huang and told him to “work hard.” The president posted on Truth Social that Huang’s return was necessary to “ensure the success and prosperity” of the American economy and that the US Attorney General determined that Huang had not broken the law.

Returns on the return

Wall Street reacted to Huang’s return almost as excitedly as your dog reacts to your coming home from an eight-hour workday:

  • Nvidia’s stock shot up more than 31% yesterday, buoying shares of data center and memory chip companies.
  • While some analysts lauded the rally as a tech trade rebound after last week’s meltdown, others cautioned that such a sharp upswing is typical of a bear market and that it could reverse.

More Jensen jubilation: Several Silicon Valley heavyweights like Elon Musk celebrated Huang’s return, and employees chanting Huang’s name greeted him at Nvidia headquarters.

Not giving Huang a hero’s welcome…many lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, who derided his reinstatement, with some questioning the national security implications. They vowed to investigate whether Nvidia violated export controls and compromised national security under his leadership.

Looking ahead: Huang is due to testify before Congressional committees next month. Meanwhile, the Commerce Department added Megaspeed, the Singaporean company that employed Huang’s paramour Alice Huang, to its trade blacklist, restricting its access to chips.—SK

items.title: CrowdStrike will spend $44b to solidify AI defenses
items.summary: Morning Brew Inc. Amid ongoing cybersecurity worries, CrowdStrike has agreed to purchase the cloud security firm Zscaler for $43.9 billion in an all-stock deal that combines two industry leaders. Each company’s shares went in different directions yesterday—CrowdStrike fell 9%…
items.author: Dave Lozo
items.contentHtml:
Amid ongoing cybersecurity worries, CrowdStrike has agreed to purchase the cloud security firm Zscaler for $43.9 billion in an all-stock deal that combines two industry leaders. Each company’s shares went in different directions yesterday—CrowdStrike fell 9%, while Zscaler soared 18%.

With everything from refrigerators to a bank being hit by AI-fueled hacks in recent weeks, businesses are racing to bolster their defenses before they become the next victims. CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz said that the merger between two companies with a combined market cap of ~$250 billion is a “path to become the largest AI safety and security company the world has ever seen.”

Here’s how these companies fit together:

  • CrowdStrike’s forte is “endpoint security,” aka services that protect computers and mobile devices.
  • Zscaler’s speciality is cloud-based products designed to replace VPNs and help businesses protect themselves against online threats.

Security companies are so hot right now: In 2024, Cisco bought cybersecurity outfit Splunk for $28 billion, Google completed a $32 billion acquisition of cloud security company Wiz last year, and CrowdStrike rival Palo Alto Networks has gobbled up several security and AI businesses, including a $25 billion purchase of CyberArk that closed earlier this year.

Looking ahead: CrowdStrike projects $500 million in annual savings within 18–24 months of the deal closing, which is expected to happen by mid-2027.—DL

items.title: 🎙️ How I AI: OpenClaw for executives: Automate every 1% annoyance
items.summary: OpenClaw for executives: Automate every 1% annoyance | Ankit Maheshwari (Innovaccer) Listen now on YouTube • Spotify • Apple Podcasts Brought to you by: Parallel —Web search built for AI scale GiveDirectly —Send cash to the world’s poorest Ankit Maheshwari is the CTO of…
items.author: Lenny Rachitsky
items.contentHtml:
OpenClaw for executives: Automate every 1% annoyance | Ankit Maheshwari (Innovaccer)

Listen now on YouTube • • Apple Podcasts

Brought to you by:

  • Parallel—Web search built for AI scale

  • GiveDirectly—Send cash to the world’s poorest

Ankit Maheshwari is the CTO of Innovaccer and the creator of a personal AI chief of staff he runs through OpenClaw on a Mac Mini. In this episode, he shows how his Jarvis handles work approvals, orders lunch, calls coworkers who miss Slack messages, books restaurants, and controls his smart home. He also explains how he uses soul files, specialist subagents, and strict guardrails to make the system trustworthy, and why he is testing local models against a $500 to $600 monthly Anthropic bill.

Biggest takeaways:

  1. The best reason to stick with an agent platform is control, not habit. Ankit remains on OpenClaw because it can use his credentials, act on his behalf, and complete tasks without requesting permission at every step. That autonomy is an architectural advantage, not brand loyalty.

  2. Start with the bottleneck, not the grand vision. Ankit’s first automation was a cron job that runs every four hours and briefs him on every resume awaiting approval, including candidate pedigree and GitHub history. Once it worked, he began spotting similar bottlenecks throughout his day.

  3. Specialized agents outperform generalist ones once the workload becomes complex. Ankit’s master agent struggled to maintain the right persona across restaurant bookings and coworker check-ins. Moving voice calls to a dedicated agent improved consistency and clarified the split between orchestration and execution.

  4. Configuring soul files requires more work than integrations. The hardest part was defining each agent’s personality, boundaries, permissions, and routing logic through files such as soul.md. Getting those instructions right required more iteration than connecting the underlying tools.

  5. Guardrails should cover the worst case before it happens. OpenClaw once approved expiring travel requests while Ankit was in transit, using the same budget and customer-impact criteria he would have applied. The decisions were sound, but the experience exposed other actions, such as job-role approvals, that needed explicit limits.

  6. The model bill is worth optimizing before the system becomes indispensable. Jarvis costs Ankit roughly $500 to $600 per month on Opus 5.5. Early tests suggest a nearly free local model can handle summaries, email, cron checks, and call orchestration, while complex browser work still requires a frontier model.

  7. The “1% annoyance” rule is an effective way to discover automations. If a task is even slightly frustrating and repeats a few times, Ankit automates it. That approach led to agents for lunch ordering, unanswered Slack messages, home automation, and potentially even calling the elevator.

  8. A terminal-first approach can keep agent building surprisingly simple. Ankit set up OpenClaw by opening its terminal interface and speaking to it like a new employee. When coding was required, OpenClaw launched Claude Code and managed the implementation itself.

  9. Teach agents the messy details, then let them keep learning. Ankit’s lunch agent confirms his order at 9:30 a.m. and acts independently if he does not respond. After one correction about ordering curry without bread, it learned both when to add bread and when a meal already includes it.

Blog and detailed workflow walkthroughs from this episode:

How I Built a Personal AI Chief of Staff With OpenClaw: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/how-i-built-a-personal-ai-chief-of-staff-with-openclaw
↳ Create an Automated Approval Digest to Clear Your Bottlenecks: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/create-an-automated-approval-digest-to-clear-your-bottlenecks
↳ Improve AI Agent Reliability by Creating Narrowly-Scoped Specialists: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/improve-ai-agent-reliability-by-creating-narrowly-scoped-specialists
↳ Automate Your Daily Lunch Order with a Personal AI Agent: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/automate-your-daily-lunch-order-with-a-personal-ai-agent

If you’re enjoying these episodes, reply and let me know what you’d love to learn more about: AI workflows, hiring, growth, product strategy—anything.

Catch you next week,
Lenny

items.title: What happens when AI splits up your friend group?
items.summary: In San Francisco, Julie Krafchick, co-host of “ The Psychology of Relationships ,” was working on podcast episodes and researching how people connect , but still keeping up with friends in media and tech. In some friend circles, you were falling behind if you weren’t using AI…
items.author: Elise Leise
items.contentHtml:
In San Francisco, Julie Krafchick, co-host of “The Psychology of Relationships,” was working on podcast episodes and researching how people connect, but still keeping up with friends in media and tech. In some friend circles, you were falling behind if you weren’t using AI models to “10x” your life and work. In others, dinner talk consisted of debates over whether The New York Times or Granta had published AI-generated work. 

Krafchick was torn. On one hand, she could see AI’s potential; she’d had a career in tech. But in both circles, she found herself deliberating how and when to talk about AI. In one exchange, a friend told her how her latest Claude project was something she had “put her heart and soul” into. 

But Krafchick didn’t necessarily view AI that way. “Personally, I want to do [creative] work,” she told Big Think. “I want to get my hands wet. So there can be a divide…when it almost feels like your friend is taking a shortcut.” Part of her felt she had worked for years to master the craft, only to have someone else “put in a prompt.” 

Still, it felt a bit dramatic to question her friend’s choice. “I do feel like this is something that…does feel like an off-limits topic,” she added. “You wonder: Why am I getting upset about AI and someone using it?” 

A new taboo

If you’ve ever felt like AI is a fraught topic, you’re not alone. You likely have at least one connection who, by virtue of their age, occupation, or feelings about the tech industry, disagrees strongly with your stance on artificial intelligence. Although AI use continues to rise, a Bentley-Gallup survey from July found that, compared with recent years, more Americans now say AI causes more harm than good, especially young adults, who are roughly split on the issue. 

Fundamentally, these friendship disagreements make sense. Like finance, politics, or sex, AI is one of those topics that holds a multitude of sensitive spots underneath. Did you study for a decade in a field threatened by AI? Are you jealous of your friend who’s set to make millions? Do you hate its use of environmental resources? Are you heavily invested in AI stocks? Often, a theoretical “AI” conversation rapidly triggers personal, practical feelings about its impact. 

Complicating things, friends may cover up their use of AI, depending on the degree to which they think others will accept it. As Sarah Newman, Director of Art & Education at Harvard University’s metaLAB, discovered when she started collecting anonymous confessions from strangers, more people than you may think have “guilty AI secrets,” or ways in which they use AI they don’t feel comfortable fully admitting in public. Should you ask your friend if they generated your wedding speech? What happens if you receive an AI-written apology text? And what if you’re ethically opposed to the AI industry and your friend goes to work at Anthropic? 

Most of the time, friends stay quiet. Even though there are plenty of reasons why AI use is such a high-tension topic — environmental ethics, copyright, and AI layoffs, to name a few — “it almost feels weird,” Krafchick explained, “to confront it.” 

Overrelying on AI

Thanks to her podcast, Krafchick is on the front lines of AI-related friendship debates. For one, AI-mediated advice is making it hard to disagree without behind-the-scenes influence. Friends turn to chatbots to talk through conflicts in friend groups, or even forward AI transcript logs to prove their point. “You’ve probably seen that before with friend groups,” she told Big Think. “People…will just copy and paste.” It’s that sense of: “Claude told me this, so it must be right.” 

As Yael Schonbrun, a clinical psychologist and the author of Why Don’t You Understand Me? The Surprising Science Behind Connecting in a World of Missed Signals, explained that heavy AI use between friends can ultimately chip away at both authenticity and trust. When we use LLMs to edit and “make what we say and think kind of refined,” she pointed out, we risk losing the vulnerability that makes a friendship work. 

Other times, friends may turn to AI to smooth over a conflict, especially if a situation is tense and they don’t know what to say. Asking a friend whether they used AI to craft a message is uncomfortable, but so is not knowing. “When you get a text that almost feels overly polished,” Krafchick told Big Think, “you’re like, ‘Did AI write this or did you write this?’” 

Not everyone, of course, wants to automate friendship. “Some of the best parts of friendship are the wildly inefficient/random/silly texts,” Meagan Phelan, a communications director at Science Journals & Publishing, wrote in response to the launch of AI-integrated text messages. She chalked the value of thoughtful check-ins up to intention, noting that taking away those tiny moments is “a very efficient way to become worse at being a friend.” 

Over time, consistently using AI to communicate can alienate and divide friend groups, especially if one or more people feel like their friends aren’t putting in personal effort. “There’s a larger conversation we need to have,” Schonbrun said, “about the way that AI fits into our relationships.” 

But friendship breakups can’t be the only way forward. So what might it take to get past our initial discomfort and have better conversations? 

A more constructive debate 

Part of the answer seems to be interrogating our own assumptions, taking time to articulate our viewpoints, and leading with curiosity rather than judgment. 

While an AI model can help us understand a friend’s point of view or express our feelings less confrontationally, Krafchick pointed out, from a friendship perspective, it’s typically best to avoid letting AI provide a word-for-word script. If “one friend goes to AI…and then they figure out what to say to the second because AI has given them [the exact words],” she elaborated, that’s when the debate starts to feel “disingenuous.” 

Instead, Schonbrun and Krafchick suggest we approach the conversation with our own words, and get curious. If you disagree, why does your friend feel that way? Are there any potential areas of overlap? What have they read or watched that they think best explains their reasoning behind a take? What’s been their personal experience? And finally — if you ever want to talk about it in a social context — what are their boundaries and how would they like to talk about it? 

In Krafchick’s friend group, the choice isn’t “AI or no AI” so much as it is chatting with the friends she’s with about ideas that catch their interest. Sometimes that’s AI; sometimes it’s not. If she’s at Sunday brunch, she might be fascinated by conversations about how AI might shape relationships moving forward, but less so by talk centered on building agents. “It’s finding what topic within AI makes sense for you,” she added.

While AI models are increasingly used as both advisor and friend, Schonbrun explained, they don’t replace the intimacy of a real friendship. If anything, they create a false expectation of how friendships — the kind that challenge and inspire us — are supposed to work. “We need to have a stake in the game in order for relationships to have depth,” she told Big Think. “For them to grow, [and] for us to be able to grow along with them.”

items.title: Euclid’s newest release unveils a cosmic treasure trove
items.summary: Back on July 1, 2023, ESA’s Euclid space telescope launched . This Falcon 9 rocket launch from July 1, 2023, carried the ESA’s Euclid mission into space. The Euclid space telescope, after deployment, commissioning, and calibration, has begun mapping out the Universe, and will…
items.author: Ethan Siegel
items.contentHtml:
Back on July 1, 2023, ESA’s Euclid space telescope launched.

This wide-field observatory is currently imaging and mapping out huge, 3D volumes of the Universe.

Alongside SPHEREx, Roman, and the ground-based Vera Rubin Observatory, Euclid heralds a cosmological revolution.

Its two main science goals are to probe dark energy’s and dark matter’s properties.

It accomplishes this by mapping out enormous numbers of galaxies across 14,000 degrees of sky.

Galaxy clustering information, in 3D space, reveals how likely galaxies are to be separated by specific distances.

A key clustering distance scale — the acoustic scale — reveals dark matter’s properties.

Complementarily, weak lensing — apparent shape distortion by foreground masses — reveals how cosmic structure grows.

Via the growth of this structure, we can probe dark energy’s nature.

Euclid, covering 14,000 square degrees cumulatively, also yields a broad range of astronomical phenomena.

Spectroscopic capabilities pin down the redshifts of distant galaxies.

Strong lenses magnify background objects, particularly within rich galaxy clusters.

Some 15,000 galaxy-galaxy strong lens candidates also appear.

Superclusters abound: containing dozens of individual galaxy clusters apiece.

Rare objects, like ring galaxies, abundantly appear.

Additionally, novel, rare, faint features appear even in well-studied galaxies.

An ongoing website, EPOD, highlights Euclid’s picture of the day.

Mostly Mute Monday tells an astronomical story in images, visuals, and no more than 200 words.

items.title: Copper prices are down. That might be a bad sign
items.summary: Wojtek Radwanski/Getty Images The copper market is in disarray, and the penny was officially removed from production on Friday. Coincidence? Actually, yes. Copper’s recent downturn has more than numismatists worried, as analysts believe it signals that the job market…
items.author: Holly Van Leuven
items.contentHtml:
The copper market is in disarray, and the penny was officially removed from production on Friday. Coincidence? Actually, yes. Copper’s recent downturn has more than numismatists worried, as analysts believe it signals that the job market, manufacturing, and the S&P 500 may be headed for declines.

“Flashing a death cross”

That’s not a reference to gang activity in GTA VI. A death cross is a technical pattern in finance trends that can be “a warning sign for economic growth,” as Renaissance Macro put it. Currently, the Bloomberg Industrials Metal Index, which is 40% copper, is flashing one.

Since copper is used in home construction, auto manufacturing, and data center buildouts, that’s not a great sign:

  • “When people build, buy, and invest, the order for copper is among the first to be placed. When they stop, it is among the first to be canceled,” economist Henrik Zeberg recently wrote on Substack.
  • He also said that a poor job market can correlate with a weak copper market because “a household that worries about its job does not buy a car or a house.”

On Friday, copper cost about $5.48 a pound, down from $6.89 in September.

Another driver of the falling prices, however, may be the (fading) spectre of new tariffs. There is currently no levy on raw copper being imported into the US. But President Trump’s repeated threats of enacting one since retaking office led companies to stockpile the metal stateside over the past two years:

  • The recent blue wave, widely interpreted as a rebuke of Trump’s economic policies, along with the pressure Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick faces over his role in the Nvidia–Megaspeed scandal, has industry watchers betting the raw copper tariff won’t come to pass after all, contributing to lower prices.

No better than bullion: Gold prices are also down, and the AI stock sell-off is partly to blame. Not every investor is selling out at a profit—some are cutting their losses, and when they do, Fast Company said, they tend to liquidate assets like gold to cover them.—HVL

items.title: Maldon Salt accused of flaky behavior
items.summary: Philip Kinsey/Adobe Stock Maldon Salt is in a bit of a pinch. The artisanal British brand—beloved by chefs everywhere for its fancy, flaky sea salts—has been peppered with questions since The Observer claims to have discovered that the salt may not be as authentic as its…
items.author: Brendan Cosgrove
items.contentHtml:
Maldon Salt is in a bit of a pinch. The artisanal British brand—beloved by chefs everywhere for its fancy, flaky sea salts—has been peppered with questions since The Observer claims to have discovered that the salt may not be as authentic as its reputation suggests.

What happened: On its website, Maldon claims it’s been harvesting its famous sea salt flakes by hand in the UK since 1882, but The Observer…observed trucks full of imported German rock salt arriving at the company’s production facility, prompting an explanation from Maldon. The company defended its process, but acknowledged it could have been more up-front about how the German rock salt factors into things.

Deepflake technology?

Maldon explained that it takes local seawater, filters it through the rock salt to create a brine, lets it evaporate, then hand-harvests the flakes left behind. And since the imported salt is from an ancient sea, it’s still technically 100% sea salt, even if the sea dried up in prehistoric times.

Salt burn: Still, some customers weren’t thrilled to hear that they’ve been stunting on their friends with dried-rock-salt brine this whole time. And if people start viewing Maldon as less than premium, it could hurt their bottom line. According to the New York Times:

  • One 8.5-ounce box of Maldon Sea Salt Flakes costs about $13.
  • From March 2024 to March 2025, Maldon made $51 million in global revenue.

Big picture: Neither British nor US regulators have a hard-and-fast definition of sea salt.—BC

items.title: The most important question you’ll ask 1,000 times a day
items.summary: You are able to make good decisions about how to live your life. I hate to open a new newsletter with a twee self-help aphorism covered in fortune cookie crumbs, but it’s probably the most important thing to start with. Because Epicureanism is an ancient Greek philosophy, and…
items.author: Jonny Thomson
items.contentHtml:
You are able to make good decisions about how to live your life.

I hate to open a new newsletter with a twee self-help aphorism covered in fortune cookie crumbs, but it’s probably the most important thing to start with. Because Epicureanism is an ancient Greek philosophy, and like almost all its contemporaries, it places responsibility on you. You are the overseer of your life. You can think things through, make good choices, and get things right. You are not some child, carried about by adult hands, blinking at a world blurring by. In the eyes of Greek philosophers, you are a rational, intelligent, deliberative human being. You control your life.

Epicureanism argues that a good life is one where we develop strategies to either cure or endure pain — both physical and emotional — while seeking out opportunities to enjoy ourselves more. It says that a happy life means savoring simple pleasures where you are, right now, and with the people who matter. But to do that, we need to make better decisions. We need to willfully choose an Epicurean life. We need to work at happiness.

Some of you might be wondering why there’s a cute little crab scuttling along our freshly minted logo. Well, that’s a hermit crab. In my upcoming book, The Art of Enough, I use the hermit crab motif to represent one of the most important ideas in Epicureanism. Because I think it embodies a certain skill we all need to nurture if we are to live a good life.
